subsubtopic: MANITOBA SEAFOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege may I say that in today's Ottawa Citizen it is reported that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) tendered a dinner, and I quote:
. . . given for the express purpose of getting members from Canada's "seagoing" provinces better acquainted.
There were Liberals from British Columbia, the Yukon, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island.
My point of privilege, sir, is that Manitoba should have been included as a "seagoing" province. Since she has a coastline almost equal to that of the province of British Columbia, she should have been included as a Canadian maritime province. I have visited many of the world's seagoing ports, as far as the east coast of Africa, and I assure hon. members that the facilities of the port of Churchill, and the port of Churchill itself, compare favourably with anything else I have seen. The disadvantages have been well advertised, but not the advantages. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the Minister of Fisheries, and to hon. members from the maritime provinces of Canada, that before this parliament terminates the members of the maritime province of Manitoba, including my good friend the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward), will tender to them an invitation to a seafood dinner, of which the piece de resistance will be white whale steak, caught in Hudson bay and processed in the great salt-water port of Churchill.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, November 2, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Thatcher.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned yesterday I had quoted a Canadian Press dispatch which had appeared in the Ottawa Citizen. I was drawing attention to the trend in Great Britain and other countries in the sterling bloc to seek commodities from other than dollar countries-in other words, to seek them in the areas where supplies were available. I mentioned such things as newsprint, bacon, eggs, timber, and so on. In the same edition of the Citizen was an editorial which I should like to place on Hansard. It reads:
A forward step in British colonial administration is the establishment of university colleges in the West Indies, Nigeria, and the Gold Coast. These have completed their first teaching sessions. Emphasis is on practical studies like rural science, so that graduates may accelerate the economic development of the colonies.
Those two articles show quite clearly the desire of Great Britain to break away from the dollar areas in purchasing her requirements, and to find these elsewhere. This curtailment may affect us considerably in the near future. In pursuance of this policy, Great Britain has developed large areas in Africa for the growing of groundnuts, which play a great part in the economy of the country. By developing these lands and seeking new markets in sterling areas, the British

The Budget-Mr. Jones are following a logical course from their point of view. These facts are too selfevident to need further emphasis.
Our position is just as clear and simple. We must put up a fight to retain the British market, and we must do so before it is too late. I was pleased to see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is taking a progressive step to retain the last segment of this market by arranging a contract for $3 million worth of apples. While this is going to cost the Canadian people some money in the current year, I think in the long run we shall gain through retaining a market that is one of the best markets British Columbia ever had. The fruit growers in my district are pleased with the action taken by the government, and would welcome any further action that would make this market a permanent one. I believe the amendment to the amendment would have that effect and I appeal to hon. members on both sides of the house to support it. As I see it, the situation calls for urgent action.
Another subject I should like to deal with is one that was raised a short while ago by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), who referred to the tremendous growth in population in British Columbia during the past few years. This has brought a considerable problem in its wake, one being the increased cost of education to the municipalities. Many of the British Columbia municipalities find themselves unable to keep a reasonable balance between the cost of education and other services needed in a community, such as roads, sidewalks, light, power, sewers, and so on.
The first charge on a municipality is that of providing educational facilities; then if there is anything left it is used to provide the other services. As I say, this unusual growth of population in British Columbia has placed an unfair burden on some of the municipalities. In some cases the municipalities are left with insufficient funds to carry out immediately necessary projects such as waterworks. Many of them have borrowed to the legal limit of around twenty per cent, and of necessity have had to leave undone many essential works that may be needed, such as sewers, waterworks, roads and so on.
I have in mind one very progressive municipality in my riding, the town of Enderby. The officials wrote to me a short time ago and pointed out that that municipality had been faced with the usual growth of population throughout the province. They stated that their education costs were worrying them, because they had had to increase their school accommodation, as well as the teachers' salaries. The general cost of education has gone up in the district. On top of all this


they have to build a new hospital. This could not be avoided, because the old one was simply a firetrap and completely obsolete. They are now compelled to renew their waterworks. Enderby is not a very large town, and during the war, or even before the war, they were in difficulties. They were in difficulties in the thirties, and the government helped them out. Therefore their credit would not be considered the best. Today they must have a new waterworks plant which will cost $178,000. It is a must. They have written me asking whether I know of any means by which they can get money from the dominion government. I made inquiries, and found that no such funds are available. I also discovered that there is an act under which something might be done to assist them. It is the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, under which municipalities were allowed to borrow money at two per cent for self-liquidating projects. Under it $30 million were made available for municipalities. Up to date $7 million have been used; the remaining $23 million were frozen by action of the government in 1940, when further access to the fund was denied. In the first place I believe it was a mistake to deny access to it. I understand that the fund was reopened for the benefit of the province of Quebec, which borrowed money for three or four years afterwards. It was a good act. I am going to ask the government to reconsider making it operative again, and thus give a break to the municipalities.
The position of the municipalities today in a province such as British Columbia is almost as serious as it was during the depression. They must grow, and they must have the facilities to take care of that growth. They must look after the health of their people, and they must have access to money bearing reasonable interest. Self-liquidating loans of this type are a sound financial investment; but more than that, they would bring untold returns by way of improvement in the health and general economy of the community. This is particularly so in the case of towns such as Enderby, which need more than the legal amount they are allowed under the municipal act, or possibly more than they could get on the open market.
I would not advocate the making of loans to the same extent as was done twenty or thirty years ago. I have in mind one town in the province of British Columbia which was compelled to borrow money over a fifty year period. After eighteen years the project for which the money was borrowed had no asset value whatsoever. It happened to be wood stave pipe. For thirty years following the loss of use of the project they had to continue to pay interest at the rate of six

per cent. I am not referring to projects of that kind; I have in mind self-liquidating projects which will return the money to the government within a reasonable number of years.
These municipalities do not expect charity. They are not willing to accept assistance of that kind, but they do seek a fair break in getting access to this money. I would go further and suggest that sound self-liquidating projects of this nature should be able to borrow money anywhere at two per cent, directly from the Bank of Canada, if you wish. After all, the wealth of Canada is not in bank credits but in the numerous progressive communities of our land. It is in our wheat fields, our mines and our timber. To my mind, the function of the Bank of Canada is to make funds available at a low interest rate in order to promote the development of these areas, thereby adding more tangible wealth to our economy. I think that the rules governing the operation of the Bank of Canada should be altered if there is to be substantial immigration to Canada in the near future. With access to that money we could have the 500,000 houses we need, and also the municipal improvements that we seek.
During the last war, British Columbia municipalities prepared plans for rehabilitation and reconstruction of their communities. The plans called for the expenditure of millions and millions of dollars, and the assumption was that the government would make funds available at a low rate of interest. So far as I know, most of them are still in abeyance. To my knowledge the bulk of the plans were sound; they were prepared by qualified engineers, right down to the blueprint stage so that they were ready to proceed. I am satisfied that unless the government change their present policy and make this money available, these plans will remain in abeyance for all time to come, because they call for a greater expenditure than any participating municipality could borrow legally on the open market.
I should like to point out that the government is doing its utmost to speed up the housing plans of the dominion. Criticism has been levelled against the government for not acting rapidly enough. I believe it is folly for the government to accelerate the construction of houses unless the municipalities in which the houses are to be built are assisted in securing the facilities necessary to service them. That is why places such as Enderby must have access to funds to which I have referred.
In Hansard of June 11, 1947, both the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair)
The Budget-Mr. Jones made valuable contributions in discussing the merits of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. I do not intend to quote from their speeches, but anyone who has any doubt about the merits of the legislation, and the benefits to be derived therefrom, can read the record. It is true that the act was designed to meet emergent conditions created by the depression, and that the conditions today are somewhat different. Speaking generally, this may be true, but fast growing municipalities are faced with the same problems of finance now as those which confronted them during the depression. The municipalities to which I refer are those which were incorporated and laid out for a population of from three to four thousand, and which now suddenly find themselves compelled to take care of a population of eight to ten thousand people without a single acre of new land being added to their taxable areas. One drawback is that the area of land within the municipality does not grow according to the increase in population. Assessment values, therefore, do not increase sufficiently to compensate for the population increase.
Having regard to the limited area incorporated, the argument may be advanced that the dominion government has no direct responsibility to assist these municipalities. May I point out that the average municipality carries between twenty and twenty-five per cent of its property tax free. Of course that includes churches and dominion and provincial public buildings. The cost of providing services to these tax-free assessible properties is carried by the other seventy-five or eighty per cent of the population who pay taxes. Many of these buildings are the property of the dominion government. I was pleased to hear the suggestion made-although not a promise-that money may be available to compensate municipalities for the services they provide to public buildings. These buildings receive, and expect to receive, police protection, road protection, fire protection, sewer and water services, and they would be the first to kick if they did not get them.
The other reason why the dominion government should assist municipalities is a simple one. In my riding we have a dominion experimental farm. Naturally there are children living there, and there is no dominion government school for them to attend. They attend the school at Summerland. The school board quite rightly feel that the dominion government should assist by taking care of some of the cost of educating children whose parents do not pay taxes because they live on dominion government experimental farm land. The same could be said of caretakers and others living on dominion government premises whose children attend school. The

The Budget-Mr. Jones principle is not new, because already this government takes care of the cost of educating the Indian children who attend the very same schools.
When all these things are considered, it will be seen that the dominion has a direct interest in the welfare of the municipalities; therefore I feel justified in asking the government to bring into operation the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. Under this legislation a municipality could borrow a portion of the $30 million on a pro rata basis, in relation to the population of the dominion. In other words a town of 3,000 could borrow approximately $9,000, and so on. But the legislation also contained a clause under which a municipality which might not qualify otherwise could borrow up to $200,000, an amount far greater than would be available on a per capita basis. It may be necessary to broaden the act to provide a far larger amount for distribution than $30 million, but I do feel that in this act the government have an instrument that should not be withheld at the present time. Either make use of it and distribute the remaining $23 million, or broaden the act and carry it even further. I understand that one province would not take advantage of this legislation when it was available; but if no other province wants it,
I think I can say on behalf of the British Columbia members that we should be glad to take the whole $23 million for municipal improvements in our province, though I understand the maritimes would like some of the money also.
Before concluding my remarks on this subject I would point out that no municipality which borrowed money under that act is in default with respect to either principal or interest, though most of the municipalities which took advantage of it were regarded by the orthodox finance houses as being on the borderline of sound finance.
I want to deal with one other subject, and in doing so to make a suggestion to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann).
I have been receiving quite a number of letters from people in my riding who have a member of the family taking medicinal drugs, originally under the supervision of a doctor but later, presumably after a period of training, being permitted to take them without going either to the doctor or to the hospital. Sometimes the cost of these drugs is very heavy. In one instance I had brought to my attention it costs $60 a month, or $700 a year, for the drug in question; but when they claim exemption in respect of income tax they are refused. On the other hand if the person concerned had the same amount added to his doctor's or hospital bill, it would be allowed as an exemption. I merely ask the


minister to consider changing the act so that anyone who is so unfortunate as to be obliged to take these drugs and to meet these heavy expenditures, while not directly under the supervision of a doctor or hospital, may claim the same exemption that would be granted if these amounts were added to the bill of the doctor or the hospital.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the budget I wish to deal with only a limited number of points that arise in this connection, since in fact this budget was under discussion earlier this year as well as during the present session. The figures before us are virtually the same as those which were under consideration earlier in the year. We must recognize that in most cases a large part of the expenditure already has been made and that the government is committed to those expenditures; no practical result, therefore, can follow from suggesting substantial changes in any of these items.
There are, however, certain aspects of this budget which should be of particular concern to members of this house at this time. As we look through the estimates which give the detailed amounts covered by the budget as a whole we find that the Department of National Defence spends more than any other single operating department of government. For that reason alone, if there were no other, it would be the duty of every hon. member, before passing upon the budget as a whole, to examine carefully how that very large amount is being spent.
Expenditures for national defence take on a new importance in view of the fact that Canada has assumed responsibilities in connection with the preservation of peace. It has been said in this house on a number of occasions that the hope for peace depends upon the combined strength of the free nations joined in the Atlantic security pact, and therefore the estimates before us have a special meaning at this time. But apart from the importance which may be attached to these estimates for that reason, there is the fact that the taxpayers of Canada are being called upon to spend nearly $400 million on national defence during the current financial year. It is the duty of hon. members of this house to take whatever steps may be regarded as necessary to ensure that this enormous sum will be properly expended and put to the best possible use for the purposes for which it is asked.
The actual estimates for the Department of National Defence amount to $375 million, but with the supplementary estimates and civilian expenditures associated with national defence activities we can take the round figure of $400 million as the amount to be expended this year by the taxpayers of

Canada on the defence of their country and as one of the member nations of the North Atlantic security pact. For this reason the members of this house who are considering the expenditure of these large sums should at the earliest moment give full consideration to the meaning of the Mainguy report- especially when one examines the purpose of these expenditures and the effectiveness of them. Requests have been made on a number of occasions for a standing committee on national defence. Such a committee has not yet been set up, and on different occasions the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has indicated an unwillingness to set it up. If there ever was a doubt in the minds of the members of this house that there should be a committee of this house on national defence, it would be removed by a careful reading of the Mainguy report.
It is necessary to remember that this report does not cover the function of the navy as part of our national defence organization. It deals with a limited part of the activities of the navy, as is indicated in the opening part of the report. On the first page, in their submission to the Minister of National Defence, the commissioners state that their conclusions are unanimous. Then they go on to say:
In an attempt to assist you, the government of Canada and the officers administering the Royal Canadian Navy, we were requested to find out and record what happened on the occasion of each of the incidents of alleged mass insubordination which occurred in the three ships concerned. We were further instructed to make appropriate recommendations, if we reached the conclusion that there were things which could and should be done to improve conditions of service, the relations between officers and men, the machinery for the ventilation of grievances and other collateral matters. We were also asked to consider whether there should be changes in regulations, conditions of service, and the training of naval personnel.
That indicates the positive limitations of this inquiry. The Mainguy report is so far-reaching, and so important in what it presents to the members of this house, as well as to the people of Canada, that we could well bear in mind that as to the organization of the navy for the particular duties assigned to it, the suitability of the ships, and the general composition of our naval forces, we receive no information. The report deals with the limited problem that was placed before the commission. I think it is proper to say that the commissioners have, by their report, demonstrated the value of inquiries of this kind. It shows what can be done in a constructive way to advance the defence services of this country by exposing to public examination those things which the people of Canada should know, and particularly, and above all, which the members of this parliament, the supreme
The Budget-Mr. Drew authority for expenditures of this type and for the organization of our defence forces, should know.
The report deals with a number of subjects. I should like to refer to some of the findings, because they have a direct bearing on the discussions that have taken place from time to time on the general problem of national defence.
On page 10 referring to consideration of the situation on board H.M.C.S. Magnificent, the report has this to say:
The complaints concerned unsanitary conditions and the presence of bedbugs, defective showers, overcrowding and inadequate arrangements for latecomers at meals. There was some ground for all these complaints. It was apparent that some of the matters complained of were adjusted. Overcrowding could not be dealt with at all during the cruise. Some fumigating was done to make the living quarters more sanitary. We are of the opinion that a good deal more of explanation could have been given of the reasons why some things could not be done. Reference has been made to the alleged lack of the proper planning of aircraft operations. It is true that a number of flights were cancelled for reasons which were not apparent to the men concerned. Apparently the aircraft handlers took some pride in their work and were quite willing to do extra tasks if they knew they contributed to the objects of the cruise. They felt that some of the changes were capricious, whereas many of them could have been easily explained but were not. The medical evidence suggested that some of the unhappiness and restlessness on board a ship which everyone called "unhappy" could be attributable to the tropical heat to which many of the men were not accustomed. This appears reasonable.
I should like to point out, in regard to this particular quotation, that all the matters to which reference is made are matters of administration, which means that, if the organization of our navy is in any way effective, they must have been brought before the Department of National Defence over and over again. If they were not, then there was a complete breakdown in the administrative organization of that department. These are conditions which any ordinary process of inspection, or any attempt to find out what was being done with extremely important equipment, would disclose very quickly.
I turn to page 41 of the report. In the intervening pages there is a tremendous amount of useful information and extremely useful recommendations. On page 41 there is a reference which may be regarded as a summary of the important recommendations contained in the report. On that page I read the words: "The Nelson tradition is overdone". No one in this country, Mr. Speaker, is more anxious than I am to see our defence organization and every aspect of our defence preparation truly Canadian, but I should think that the navy of the United States, or the navy of any other country in the world, would be proud of the Nelson tradition, which was

The Budget-Mr. Drew one of outstanding success in that great branch of the service. It is not a question of continuing to follow an ancient pattern. Nelson fought in ships under sail, and undoubtedly Nelson had an able force, recruited under very different methods from those described in this report. I am not now referring to the invention of the radio. In those days people had different views as to methods of encouraging enlistment in the armed forces of the time, but so far as the tradition was concerned, it was one which seemed to be good. I have found that our friends in the United States-and I mention the United States because we must recognize that that country provides the great central strength of our combined system of defence of the free world-at all times have been only too willing and too anxious to embrace the traditions which they inherited in earlier days from another land. I find that they study with enthusiasm the events which led to success in that branch of the service in an earlier day. But there is one Nelson tradition which in this house has been preserved. Every time an hon. member has raised some question in regard to national defence, has sought further information about it and advocated an inquiry by a committee of the house set up for the purpose, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has followed one well-known Nelson tradition; he has put the telescope to his blind eye; he has refused to see the subject that was being discussed. This particular Nelson tradition is not one that has borne very useful results in this particular case, and I think every hon. member will agree that it might well be abandoned; that we should put the telescope to the good eye and begin to appreciate these extremely important responsibilities.
I should like to refer to a statement which appears on page 42. There is the positive statement of these men that, according to the reports they received, the present actual complement of officers and men-and this was stated by several witness-was inadequate for the existing commitments and tasks of the navy if it is to concentrate on training, as it must do.
The report goes on to make certain suggestions which the commissioners believe would be helpful in meeting the situation. In the next paragraph on page 42 the report says that there are too few ships available for adequate training. My information is that certain steps have been taken to improve that situation, and that one of the ships which had been used for other purposes is now being used for training purposes.
On the next page, under the heading "Recruiting", there is a statement which has

a direct bearing on the expenditures of public money. This is what the three commissioners found:
In our opinion, and in the opinion of almost every witness, the recruiting methods were bad. Many officers complained that the organization of advertised recruiting had been left almost entirely to professional advertisers and specialists in commercial radio, who have known nothing of the navy, however skilled they may be in the sale of consumers' goods to a coy and jaded public. We propose to deal with this matter at some length, as we join with the men and officers whom we have examined in the belief that "soft soap operas" do not contain the virility, dignity and patriotic appeal which should be used to persuade young Canadians to serve their country.
That is something that every hon. member has observed. Looking at the advertisements for the navy, many people might imagine, until they read them more carefully, that they were advertisements for a world cruise in which the greatest possible comfort would be available for all who took this special opportunity. As the report points out, our young people are ready to assume their full responsibilities. They are a virile, courageous and energetic group of young people who are prepared to perform the tasks that are involved. What this report points out is to suggest that this is just some pleasant episode in which the crew are taking part creates an entirely wrong approach in seeking enlistments in the navy. The report suggests that it is desirable that an appeal be made to the real spirit of our people to take their share in the duties of nationhood. That general recommendation is one which certainly should have a bearing on the question of the continuance of some of these radio broadcasts, which give the impression that the appeal is being made for something in no way related to naval training or naval service.
On page 53 there is another reference in regard to recruiting, which follows a number of intervening pages that deal with this matter in some detail. It is as follows:
In recruiting, what is sometimes called the "bed of roses" approach, and what is sometimes called the "beer and skittles" approach should be eliminated. Naval officers themselves should be invited to take far more interest and a much greater part in recruiting campaigns. Neither the design nor the content of publicity should be left to commercial advertisers. Every naval officer examined criticized what has been done. While their criticism may be fair, their abstention from this activity in the past placed an unjust burden upon those whose duty it was to shape the programs. A consultation between naval authorities and officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would probably produce some good ideas. In any event, we have sufficient faith in the youth of Canada to believe that they will not shrink from rigours if they know they are essential to national service.
Nor do we think either, that they need to be molly-coddled before they will offer themselves in their country's needs. In the picturesque phrase of one journalist who wrote about the navy, they

will not run away from the sea it they realize that "the navy is a challenge and not a chesterfield." If they are told that the navy, while treating its men and their dependents fairly, and paying them good wages and giving them wholesome food, is nevertheless a career for a "man," hard to enter but honourable, patriotic and adventurous, we do not believe that young Canadians will fail to respond to the appeal of their country.
That is the end of the quotation, but it is a quotation which should be in the minds of all hon. members in examining the very large sums being spent on advertisements of this kind, and on the soap operas to which this report refers.
Then, at page 60 there is another item of importance in discussing this whole subject, and it comes under the heading of "Laundries". This may seem unimportant in itself, but it is very important to people who require facilities of that kind. I quote the following from page 60:
We received most vigorous evidence concerning the absence of proper laundry facilities at Esquimalt. The situation, in our opinion, demands immediate attention. In spite of frequent representation by responsible officers, over a period of years, no laundry yet exists in Esquimalt.
There is a naval laundry at Halifax. Esquimalt should be given the same facilities immediately.
The point I should like to make is that this refers to repeated representations by responsible officers. There again, if that is something that needs to be done, and has needed to be done for some years, then there is definitely some breakdown in the organization, and a breakdown in the chain of responsibility in the over-all administration of this service, if that has not been acted upon. While in this particular instance it deals with the absence of a laundry, it is quite possible a much more serious subject might receive equal treatment under the same system of administrative responsibility.
Then at page 67 we find the very strongest emphasis placed upon training that should be given in the matter of the relationship between officers and men, and the requirements of full instructions in the humanities. There, again, is something that stems from the top, and for which those in the highest position of responsibility must assume responsibility in respect of everything that has happened.
At page 70 the report deals with recreational facilities ashore, and makes this finding:
Shore facilities for the recreation, entertainment and, education of Canadian sailors are very inadequate, especially on the west coast. They are somewhat better at the east coast. Many of the men are aware of what the United States authorities do for the officers and men of their navy. We had the privilege of visiting the Seattle Naval Air Station Recreational Building at Seattle. When we compared the magnificent facilities for the playing of games, for the carrying on of hobbies, for sea bathing and for reading at Seattle with the dinghy
The Budget-Mr. Drew surroundings, the poor quarters and the lack of equipment at Esquimalt, we could not be anything but envious for our country's sake.
I feel sure that the word "dinky" is the word that was originally intended, when they refer to "dinghy surroundings". I should think "dinky" would be the only appropriate word.
