speechtext:
There is another reference at page 71 under the heading "Films at Sea" and this again makes the finding that a great deal more could be done to provide films at sea, that this whole matter should be dealt with, and that the national film board should be brought into this general picture. They say much greater use could be made of the film board, although the ordinary educational films are not popular with men at sea. I quote this statement from page 72:
Many of them told us, however, that they would be interested in travel films and particularly in films depicting life in countries to be visited on their various cruises.
Then at pages 72 and 73 we find the conclusions which, at this time, I do not propose to read in detail. However, they are conclusions which relate to the whole question of the proper expenditure of our money, and what we are getting for this enormous sum that we spend. One finding which I believe will be welcomed by every hon. member is that in paragraph (1) at page 73, which states:
We do not believe that there are any so-called "subversive" forces at work in the navy or that any such elements were responsible for the incidents. Like many other similar happenings, they passed through the usual phases of discontent, exaggeration of grievance, folly and thoughtless action.
The whole report, Mr. Speaker, is simply a finding within a limited field to the effect that there has not been effective administrative supervision of our naval services. There is no one in the house who has had contact with the members of the Royal Canadian Navy who does not realize that the personnel of that navy commands the admiration and respect of the people of Canada. It should be a matter of concern to every member in the house, wherever he sits, to make sure that appropriate steps are taken to deal with the findings in this report.
The point however which I should like to emphasize in this budget debate is this: This report opens only one window to the
1404	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Drew whole national defence department. What we see here indicates the urgent need for similar inquiry into every other aspect of our defence organization and administration in Canada. Across this country young men and women in the permanent and nonpermanent units of the navy, the army and the air force are doing a splendid job within the limitations of the opportunities afforded to them. In any one of the naval, military or air stations across Canada we can see young men and women carrying themselves in a manner that justifies the pride of every Canadian in those who wear the uniform of Canada. The least that we can do as members of parliament is to accept the responsibility of making sure that the $400 million of the taxpayers' money that is being spent for national defence is spent in the best possible way.
Nothing will contribute more effectively to the efficiency and high morale of those young men and women than to be sure that what money is being appropriated for this purpose is being put to the best possible use. I have no intention of reviewing in detail the many incidents that have occurred or going back over the discussions which have taken place in the past, but it will be recalled that in response to repeated requests for a standing committee on national defence the hon. members of this house have been given over and over again reassuring statements as to the complete efficiency of every operation in every branch of the department.
Those members of the press who had the opportunity to accompany the very small military and air forces which took part in Operation Eagle gave to the Canadian people a report which could be described only as disturbing, to use the mildest possible word. Following on the very emphatic assurances which had been given as to the quality of equipment and the readiness of certain of our forces to play their part, a report was given to the people of Canada by highly experienced veterans of the war who are now in the press service of Canada describing what could only be termed a fiasco.
This was no reflection on the men who had taken part in that operation. On the contrary, the press reports emphasized the excellent drill, the excellent spirit and the high morale of those who had taken part. But the reports emphasized also the inadequacy of the equipment and the fact that the units concerned were certainly not ready to go into action with the equipment they had. That was another small window opened to the situation in the army.
In the case of the air force, in spite of reassurances about the availability of equip-
	i, 1 SflMI

ment, the same press reporters informed the people of Canada about the inadequacy of the aircraft available for that particular operation. There again a very small window was opened through which the people of Canada could get just a peek into the actual situation in that great force.
Let no one suggest that anything that was said by these reporters was in the way of reflection upon those who are in these services today. Nowhere in the world are there men and women in uniform more capable of undertaking the tasks placed before them, but they can only do the job for which they are trained and for which they are given the essential equipment and supplies.
Without going into further details of this uniform and unanimous report of those who attended Operation Eagle, it does point to the necessity of an inquiry which will make it possible for the hon. members of this house to pass upon the estimates of the Department of National Defence with an actual knowledge of what the facts really are. Our whole free system rests upon knowledge of the facts. We do not prove that we have a working democracy merely because members representing all the constituencies in Canada are permitted to come and sit in this chamber, with the right to speak under the rules of this house. What determines whether this is really an efficient democracy is whether the members of this house are able to make their decisions with full knowledge of every essential fact in the possession of the government itself.
Perhaps because of the secrecy of the war years, which is something that no one can criticize to the extent that it became necessary, there has been a continuing tendency to regard essential information as the particular knowledge of the government unless by accident members of the opposition happen to find out about it or happen to make inquiries which bring it into the open for discussion in this chamber.
The whole history of our system demonstrates that it rests for its effectiveness upon knowledge of every essential fact, and that in peacetime the opposition-may I say hon. members supporting the government as well -are entitled to all essential information in the possession of the government. No one will question the necessity under circumstances of grave international uncertainty for some measure of secrecy-I will go further and say a high degree of secrecy-in regard to the military aspects of the development of atomic energy. But that relates to preparation of highly secret defence requirements which every hon. member of the house accepts. So far as the organization of our defence forces and their suitability for the

tasks that they may be called upon to undertake are concerned there is no reason for secrecy as to a single detail. There is no reason why every hon. member of the house should not have available to him for the purpose of reaching conclusions all information that is in the possession of the government.
This is not a new subject. Over and over again in the past the same arguments have been made, and the advances that have taken place throughout the years have been as a result of the appointment of committees of some kind which could inquire into the real requirements of our defence forces, and their efficient organization for the tasks they might be called upon the undertake. The modern army system in Great Britain, which we in Canada have followed to a considerable extent, came about as a result of the findings of the famous Esher committee of 1904. Demands have been made since the time of the South African war for an inquiry into the organization of the forces, the suitability of training, and their ability to undertake any tasks they might be called upon to perform in the future. It was not until that committee was appointed that the errors that had been so apparent in the South African war were overcome, and an effective reorganization took place under the modern general staff system. Other famous and important inquiries followed at different times. After the first world war General Otter made his famous findings known as the Otter report. In it was laid down the appropriate organization of the land defence forces of Canada, and the way in which they should be trained for the tasks they might be called upon to undertake.
It was not for some years that effective steps were taken to bring about the necessary reorganization, and in the meantime much had happened. In 1933 and 1934 extensive inquiries were conducted by the conference of defence associations, a body which embraced both permanent and non-permanent officers of the defence services of Canada. It was as a result of their recommendations that the reorganization took place which made it possible for Canada to mobilize its forces effectively at the outbreak of the last war.
Another war has passed. Four years have elapsed since it ended. The evidence is now clear on all sides that it is essential that there be an examination of the over-all plan of national defence, the suitability of the organization of our forces for that plan, the effectiveness of the training that is undertaken, and the proper expenditure of the money devoted to this purpose. There is no occasion to go into the past. We are confronted today
The Budget-Mr. Drew with the necessity of spending enormous sums of money, approximately $400 million. Only a few days ago it was indicated to us that a bill would be presented for the unification of the defence forces of Canada. Unification undoubtedly is highly desirable, but unification will not be very effective unless the forces which are unified have themselves been placed in proper relationship to other forces, having regard to what is conceived to be Canada's particular place in the general overall picture today.
It is only by the assessment of our requirements that we can know whether our money is being properly spent. It is an enormous sum of money by any standard, and every hon. member of the house has a duty to make sure that we know that it is being properly spent. If unification is to be effective, then there must first be an understanding of what the tasks are of the various forces which are to be unified under a plan of that kind. In the past few weeks we have seen a demonstration of the problems of unification. It may be worth while for us to remember that these problems were brought to the light of day by a committee where evidence was given about the organization of the defence forces, and the related requirements of the various defence services.
Many people may feel that in the Washington inquiry into certain problems of defence in the United States there was too full a discussion of various matters connected with national defence. I believe that nothing but good can come from a full discussion of that kind because the officers of the different departments were free to express their opinions, and to place before congress and the people of the United States what they regarded as the correct relationship of the army, navy and air force in their combined responsibilities. It is not a sufficient answer to say that the system in the United States is based upon committees, and that those committees initiate legislation, and initiate findings which are acted upon by the executive. I am not speaking about procedure but about the result. I am speaking about the fact that in the sister democracy of the United States members of the house of representatives and of the senate are able to make their decisions with a knowledge of the facts as placed before a committee by the highest experts of the different services of that country. After all, they did not hesitate to discuss the advantages or disadvantages of the B-36. They did not hesitate to discuss the capabilities of their most modern jet fighters. They did not hesitate to discuss the limitations of their aircraft carriers, their battleships and their cruisers. They did not hesitate to discuss the relationship of the army to the

The Budget-Mr. Drew navy and air force in the defence of freedom. Out of that discussion will come a decision based upon actual knowledge, and undoubtedly future errors which might seriously threaten their defence will be overcome by that very exchange of information and public discussion.
I know a motion could be placed upon the order paper that in the opinion of this house it is desirable that a standing committee on national defence be appointed for the purpose of considering our problems in connection with national defence. I also know that placing such a motion upon the order paper would not assure me the same opportunity to discuss this subject that is assured me at this moment. I also know that such a motion can produce no greater results if at this time the government is not prepared to accept the lesson of the Mainguy report and recognize that the time has come to appoint such a standing committee.
We had reasons given why this could not be done. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that any reason for not setting up a standing committee on national defence was swept into the discard the moment this government set up a committee on atomic energy. If it is appropriate to set up a standing committee of this house to examine the question of atomic energy, which has the very highest military potential as well as great peacetime possibilities for the welfare of society, surely it is equally appropriate that there should be a standing committee on national defence to examine the whole subject. That committee could examine our military forces to see how they should be constituted in order that we might make the very best use of our money. It could examine how the forces can be most efficiently integrated, how the minister may be best advised by his military officers, how the chain of military responsibility up to the chief of staff of each of the main services can best be carried out to avoid what was found in this recent inquiry. These are things a committee of this house can do. These are things it is the duty of members of this house to consider; and I submit that hon. members have no right to give the government a blank cheque for $400 million unless they have an opportunity to learn what really are the facts.
When I mention the figure of $400 million I recognize that at this point we cannot expect to have the appropriate information for the consideration of the estimates this year. Most of the money has been spent already. However, I do urge the government, and I do urge the minister in the interests of the efficient operation of his own department as well as in the general interests of the people of Canada, that an undertaking be

given that a standing committee on national defence will be set up this session so that it may start its work and hon. members may have some assurance of adequate information when they are called upon to consider these estimates in the session to be called in the new year. That is the only way we can have an assurance now that we will be able to fulfil our responsibilities at that time.
I do hope the minister will regard this report as something that will be helpful to him. I hope he will not be satisfied to simply tell us of the things he has done already and what he intends to do to implement the recommendations of this report. Because of what this report has disclosed I hope he will assure us that we shall have the opportunity to obtain this information, and that in addition to the officers of the department experts will be obtained who can advise that committee on the most effective way in which the money provided in the estimates may be spent upon the defence forces of this country. We want to know that this large amount is being properly spent and that the waste disclosed in the Mainguy report is not being continued over a much wider field, throughout the whole of the defence services.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer briefly to the subject matter of the amendment introduced on behalf of the opposition, to remind hon. members that we have urged that at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth be called for the purpose of doing everything possible to solve the trade problems that exist between those nations. It has been pointed out already that if we succeed in solving those problems within the commonwealth we shall have found a solution to the wider problems which confront the dollar-sterling areas today. This is a subject with which every hon. member of every party must be greatly concerned at this time. In presenting his budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) gave assurances that the government is dealing with the matter. We have placed before the house a proposal which offers one practical and effective way of dealing with this problem as it should be dealt with, at the earliest possible date. Let us find ways of tackling this question which can gain the support of all hon. members. It is not sufficient for us to have bland reassurances from the minister that this will be solved. We have a right to know how it will be solved. We have a duty to suggest how it can be solved; and we know there is a problem to solve.
I am not going to go back and read the assurances that were given just a few months ago, when members of this government told the people of Canada there was no trade

problem. I need not recall to hon. members the repeated statement by the Minister of Finance that there would be no change in the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to the United States dollar. I need not recall the fact that even the word "ridiculous" was applied to suggestions that soon we would be called upon to face this problem. There is no need to refer to those now. The ministers of this government are quite properly telling the people of Canada today that there is a crisis ahead.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No minister said there was a crisis ahead of us.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the ministers have not used that expression, then they simply failed to use an expression which properly describes what they have said. If they do not believe there is a crisis, then the proper ministers should speak to Mr. Donald Gordon, who described the crisis fully in New York a few days ago. There have been those who have suggested that this government places great reliance on the statements of Mr. Donald Gordon, and the confidence of the government in his statements has been indicated by his recent appointment. Mr. Donald Gordon gave a speech which should be reread-I do not want to suggest to the minister that he re-read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I saw it before it was delivered.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we now know that these statements by senior civil servants are, in fact, statements of government policy. In future we will bear that in mind. I believe it is important to know that the Minister of Finance saw Mr. Gordon's statement. We shall all re-read that speech in the light of that knowledge. Since the minister saw it before it was delivered, it can be taken for granted that Mr. Gordon at least wanted to know that there would not be any disapproval of what he said. If that is the case, we can examine Mr. Gordon's speech knowing that, to put it in its mildest form, the government did not disapprove of what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Finance certainly did not disapprove of what he said.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance certainly did not disapprove, and this is his budget. The Minister of Finance did not disapprove of a speech which gave a clear picture of recurring crises in the history of the world, brought us up to the present crisis, and pointed out that the only way to meet the crisis was for North America to buy more from Europe in the years ahead. It is that crisis to which I refer. If the Minister of Finance has not used the word crisis, he has certainly approved of the description of
The Budget-Mr. Drew the crisis by a senior civil servant who discussed his speech with the minister in advance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Gordon is not a civil servant.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not going to go into the definition of the appropriate description of employees of the Bank of Canada. The word "civil servant" is a word of which anybody can be proud who occupies a position in the public service. Since the Bank of Canada is an agency of the government or is presumed to be performing a public service, I would have thought the term was reasonably appropriate in this case. We need not quibble as to whether he is a civil servant. In this case, he would appear to be a government spokesman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not the case, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Although Mr. Donald Gordon before going to New York consulted with the Minister of Finance and submitted his speech to him-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Gordon, as he has done in the past, was good enough to send me a copy of his speech. I think he sent it to a great many people. I read it with interest, as I always read his speeches. It represents his own views. I happen to concur in them, but it does not represent a statement of government policy and was not put forward as such.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr Speaker, there is a clear principle involved in the statement that has just been made. Our system of government is one which accepts the proposition that the government is one, and that the statement of the appropriate minister is a statement on behalf of the whole government in regard to a matter that is the responsibility of that department. The Minister of Finance has stated that he approved Mr. Gordon's speech, so that whether he was the government's spokesman or whether he was merely putting forward his own opinion, we may read that speech with the knowledge that the Ministe; of Finance, the minister responsible for the budget statement of Canada which we are now considering, approves of that speech. We may examine it in that light.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I sometimes approve of the speeches of the leader of the opposition, but not often.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know that there have been occasions on which the Minister of Finance approved, because I was interested in hearing him repeat some of the arguments I had used about letting the Canadian dollar go to another

The Budget-Mr. Drew level when that decision was actually made. I also recognize that, in the very nature of things, we shall not always agree. I am hoping that in this particular case the Minister of Finance will agree with the proposal that has been put forward, that a positive step be taken to meet what was described in a speech that was approved by the Minister of Finance as a crisis.
If there is to be an effective solution of that problem it is essential that those who have two different parts of this problem to deal with should get together as soon as possible. There was one feature of Mr. Gordon's speech which, perhaps, does call for some attention. Mr. Gordon was speaking in New York. Undoubtedly he was really making an argument that the United States should buy more from Europe, but in using the appropriately courteous terms he used the expression "North America". Now, that expression indicates a general tendency to bracket Canada and the United States as two countries with the same dollar problem. One frequently sees clear evidence that the discussion of this subject is based, in many cases, on the idea that although we may be a nation with about one-eleventh of the population of the United States, nevertheless, standing side by side with the United States, our problem is the same.
Our problem is not the same. Our problem is a different problem and it is of vital importance to the future of Canada that we begin to deal with this problem as a different dollar problem from the United States dollar problem. Today Canada is actually at the crossroads in the relationship between the United States and Great Britain in the economic field. If we proceed to regard our problem as the same problem which confronts the United States, we may find that the United States has solved its part of the problem while we are left with no satisfactory solution. The reason our position is so different from that of the United States is that we have one striking similarity to the United Kingdom. We have a very unbalanced economy.
When I use the term "unbalanced" I do not mean adversely unbalanced, I mean the contrary. We have been expanding and developing for years, exporting far more than we import. We have been a great supplier of foodstuffs, of raw materials and of partially fabricated materials from those raw materials. In more recent years we have become a great industrial nation, and with the dramatic discoveries of oil and iron in this country in the past few years we shall become an increasingly important industrial nation. The prospects of this country were never brighter than they are today, so long

as we do not forget that we have built up our whole level of production on the basis of export. We export more than one-third of all we produce; whereas the United States exports only a very small proportion. The United States has an almost completely self-contained economy. True, they buy from us such things as paper, pulp, wood products, minerals and certain of our industrial products as well as agricultural products, but to a great extent they are self-reliant or potentially self-reliant. On the other hand, we in the northern part of this continent must buy from outside Canada huge quantities of the goods we require. No matter what our population may become we shall always be a great importing nation, and for that importation we shall depend upon enormous exports.
In discussing this subject there is one feature of our export position which we must never forget and which places us in a different position from that of the United States. Before the war our great markets were overseas. In the last few years before the war, when the impact of war preparation did not have its effect upon exports and imports, in the year 1937, out of every thousand dollars worth of exports from Canada $370 worth went to the United States, and $630 worth overseas. Of that $630 out of every thousand, $372 was paid by the United Kingdom and $104 was paid by the rest of the nations of the British commonwealth. Thus we find that out of every thousand dollars of exports to the whole world $476 was paid by the nations of the British commonwealth. That was our great export market; also, these exports were going to nations which produced many of the things that we required as well. That proportion of export business had a very important bearing on the whole internal structure of this country.
Because we have relied on overseas exports from the earliest days our rail lines, our internal shipping lines, the services associated with them and the seaports have been built up to carry our trade to the outside world, and particularly to the United Kingdom. Any substantial loss of that overseas trade cannot simply be compensated for by a corresponding amount of exports to the United States. We want the highest possible export to the United States of goods that we produce; but it would be disastrous for this country if we became entirely dependent upon the United States as the one place outside Canada where we could sell the goods we produce. That has no relationship to our friendly association with the United States. It has to do with the situation that would result from the loss of that export business. Think of what it would mean to our railways; think of what it would

mean to all these shipping services; think of what it would mean to the internal ships that carry these goods to the seaports; think of what it would mean to the people at the seaports; and think of what it would mean to the men and women working on the ships themselves which carry these goods to the different markets of the world. It would have the most serious consequences on the whole economy of Canada. Therefore one of our most urgent requirements is to find a way of meeting that problem.
Only yesterday a Canadian Press dispatch carried the story that the two Canadian representatives who visited Britain in the past couple of weeks were shocked at the severity of the cuts proposed by the British government in the purchase of Canadian foodstuffs. Today we read in the press it is expected that there will be a cut of $100 million in certain lines of foodstuffs; but what is even more serious, as we look at this picture, is that nearly all of the purchases which are now being made in the sterling area are being made with Marshall funds. Unless we take effective steps, and take them soon, to meet this problem, then we shall have found no effective way to sell to the sterling area when Marshall funds come to an end. The time, therefore, to take the steps is now, and the time to meet the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, Pakistan, Ceylon and the other partners of the commonwealth, is right now while we still have time to work out an effective solution before we are confronted with the actual withdrawal of the buying power which exists today. That is the reason for our proposal. It is the only effective way it can be done.
We have before us a subamendment calling for an over-all reduction in tariffs. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members have not before them sufficient information to vote on the subamendment with any knowledge of what the effects of it would be. Already we have had reports from different ridings of what the effect is of the differential between the revaluation of the pound and the revaluation of the dollar. The fact is that for all practical purposes the United Kingdom has reduced our tariffs by a net 20 per cent within these past few weeks. We certainly should know what the impact would be on Canada generally and on employment in Canada before we support any general resolution of this kind, no matter how sincerely desirous every one of us may be to assist the United Kingdom and the other nations of the commonwealth at this time.
We shall not have greatly contributed to the solution of this problem if we follow any course which weakens Canada at this time. It has been pointed out that in the textile
The Budget-Mr. Drew industry alone 500,000 Canadians are dependent for their livelihood on a business which is feeling the new competition. The answer to that may be given in different ways. The answer will doubtless be found by the appropriate examination of the subject bj those directly concerned in this business. But today the indication is that the manufacturers in Britain are finding it possible to sell their products here under the new circumstances. A dollar-sterling board has been set up in Canada and a dollar-sterling board has been set up in Britain for the purpose of stimulating this business.
I submit there is not sufficient evidence before the house at the present time for us to deal with a recommendation of this nature, because already we see evidence that the opportunity to sell here in Canada has been greatly changed in these past few weeks to the advantage of those in the sterling areas. All of us will certainly welcome their opportunity to sell in our markets.
I should like simply to refer to the amendment before the house, which reads:
This house regrets that the government has failed to take effective measures to prevent the present decline in our trade with the sterling area and is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of inviting the nations of the commonwealth to a conference in the immediate future for the purpose of working out arrangements to preserve and enlarge those traditional markets on which jobs and opportunities for Canadians very largely depend.
I submit that when the purpose of this amendment is examined it will be found it is one which can be supported by every member in the house; and that, in so far as any expression of regret is concerned, no member of the opposition will suggest that that is a want of confidence motion in the ordinary sense, but merely an expression of our regret that this has not yet taken place. We do urge members of the House of Commons to support this recommendation, that Canada take the initiative, with its special dollar problem, in bringing together the nations of the commonwealth to find a solution of the trading arrangements upon which the common prosperity of this great partnership will depend in the years ahead.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members will not expect me to agree with everything the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has said in his interesting speech; but with the general objective in his concluding remarks I am sure each of us would agree.
With regard to his references to the subject of national defence, and particularly to the Mainguy report, I am glad to hear him say that the report demonstrated the value of inquiries of this kind. And I might ask this

The Budget-Mr. Claxton question: Who asked that the inquiry be held? The suggestion did not come from any source except myself. Who made public the report of the inquiry when it was made?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: " 'I', said the sparrow".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I find we are on all fours with respect to some of the conclusions, but I am rather surprised that the fact that the inquiry should have been instituted, carried out effectively and promptly and resulted in such a useful report, and that this report should instantly have been made public, should not have been the subject of some word of appreciation.
May I say a word or two with respect to the report itself. At page 1 I find these words:
Without in any way controlling our activities, directing our inquiries, or attempting to shape our conclusions, you were kind enough to add to your instructions a number of most valuable suggestions. We wish to thank you for the honour of our appointment and for the helpful observations with which it was accompanied.
That is the end of this quotation from the opening passages of the report, addressed to myself.
So that hon. members may have before them some of the suggestions to which reference was made, I should like to read from a memorandum I gave to the members of the committee when it was set up. This memorandum of suggestions will show why the inquiry went into the subjects it did, and made some findings which have been surprising to hon. members. Some of their findings and their report were made in response to specific inquiries, but no effort was made to limit the scope of the report in any way whatsoever.
In this memorandum I said:
While no suggestion is made as to the form or tenor of the report, it is considered that it would be useful if its contents could cover the following questions which are included among those raised in the minds of many members of the public.
(a)	Is there any indication that any one of the incidents was the result of the action of subversive elements?
(b)	Is there any indication that any one of the incidents was planned some time in advance?
(c)	Is there any indication that the three incidents were the result of concerted action of men on two or more of the vessels? (For example, even if there was no direct evidence of this, it might appear that one or two men taking a leading part in spark-plugging the action had been together in a group at some time at Esquimalt. If there was anything in this, it might be desirable to make a detailed comparison of the service careers of at least some of the men.)
(dO In each case had any of the grievances or complaints subsequently voiced by the men been made either formally or informally to their officers? If so, had any action been taken to remove the cause of such complaints or to explain why it was undesirable or unnecessary that any action should be taken?
(e)	Is the procedure laid down for making complaints adequate, understood and used?

(f)	Is the relationship between officers and men such that the men really do go to their officers and speak frankly to them?
(g)	In each case did any of the ship's junior officers, chief petty officers, petty officers, leading seamen or other senior ratings know of the complaints or grievances before the incident? If so, what action did they take? Did they bring the matter to the attention of the appropriate authority and explain the action they were taking to the men?
(h)	Did any of the officers or senior ratings know in advance that the men were going to take the action they did?
(i)	If they did not know, how was it explained that this should be the case in view of the close and continuous association between officers, senior ratings and ratings aboard ship?
(j)	When did the men first begin to discuss the action they subsequently took? Was the action taken the result of an accumulation of grievances, whether real or imagined, or did it result from some particular incident, or was it due to a combination of a number of grievances which culminated in the action taken?
(k)	Did the men thoroughly understand the machinery for voicing grievances?
(l)	Did the men thoroughly understand the impropriety of the action they took?
(m)	What reason do the men give for not following the regular procedure?
(n)	If it is considered useful, some general reference might be made to the general character, bearing, background, training morale, sense of duty and education of the officers and men.
(o)	Reference might also be made to any relevant facts or views about the conditions of service ashore and afloat, including accommodation, food, recreation, leave, pay and allowances.
It must be quite obvious from the scope of the questions in this memorandum that the answers which might be given to some of them at least were anticipated by the officers at naval service headquarters and myself. In view of these incidents it was exceedingly important in the interest of our national defence and of our naval services to establish beyond question what the facts were, why the incidents occurred and how the conditions which gave rise to them could be met. It was not only important to find that out, but also to get from the three members of the committee which made the inquiry, a group which enjoyed the most complete respect and confidence, views on these questions which would be useful in presenting the matter to the public and which would reinforce our own efforts to see that conditions in the navy were made as good as they could be.
It is important to recall that the members of the inquiry made some general findings. On page 3 they said this:
Although this report in the very nature of things is bound to be critical, it must not be assumed that there are not many reasons for great national pride in the achievements of the Canadian navy past and present, and in the men who inherit and guard its traditions. It is certain also that wisdom, experience, and the passage of time will, by their own momentum, work many great and lasting improvements. We were asked to find out what was wrong

with the navy. If, therefore, we have stressed what is wrong, it should not be forgotten that a great deal is overwhelmingly right.
The members of the inquiry saw some 238 witnesses and in accordance with the directions that had been given they -had officers and men in and obtained their views in the frankest and freest possible way on everything relating to the incidents and the state of training and discipline and the conditions of life aboard the ships. This was done with the purpose of endeavouring to rectify a condition which clearly was wrong, and it was done with the thought that a full disclosure and a full and frank report would enable the people to judge exactly what was the situation,
I must say that the members of the inquiry did a magnificent job and in tabling the report the day before yesterday I thanked them in the name of the government for having done a great bit of work. This is more than a report dealing with certain incidents; it may well constitute an historic document dealing generally with the questions of naval traditions and discipline and the allimportant relationship of officers and men.
The report contains some thirty enumerated recommendations, but in addition there are a number of others. As I said yesterday, when the estimates of the department are under consideration I shall be glad to take up any of the points mentioned in the report and discuss them in detail with hon. members. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) referred to some seven or eight different pages in the report, but before dealing with what he said I should like to call the attention of hon. members to one significant fact that must be taken into consideration when evaluating and considering the problem of organizing the navy after the end of the war. At page 5 of the report there is a table showing the number of officers and men and the number of ships in the Canadian navy in 1939, the total personnel being 1,585 and the number of ships, 16. During the war the personnel was built up to a peak of 93,034 and the number of ships increased to 956. At the time of the report the personnel totalled 8,813 and the number of ships 54.
These figures will show hon. members something of the problem of reorganizing the Royal Canadian Navy on a post-war basis. I might say from my own knowledge that the navy has suffered one handicap in comparison with the army and the Royal Canadian Air Force in that the proportion of officers and men who were in the service before the war is smaller than is the case in the other two services. This means that the navy has fewer
The Budget-Mr. Claxton officers and men who have long experience, particularly experience of service in peacetime.
One striking fact I might mention is that the navy has increased in size some 25 per cent in the last two years, which represents a large job of training, of manning ships and settling down to the routine of working the ships. The navy has been operational to a larger degree than the other two services and unquestionably this has imposed a strain upon it, which is referred to in the report. I am not saying this by way of an answer or by way of an excuse; I say it because it is necessary in order to understand the problems that the navy has been faced with and to be fair to the officers and men who did a great job during the difficult period.
I think it would be more convenient to deal with these specific points mentioned by the leader of the opposition when the estimates are under consideration, but perhaps I should refer to some of them. He referred to the fact that on page 10 reference is made to some of the conditions on board H.M.C.S. Magnificent and expressed some surprise that the conditions there described should not have been brought to the attention of naval service headquarters or of the minister himself. Some of us have been on great ocean liners and I venture to say that we probably would not be surprised that cockroaches are occasionally found on some of the great luxury vessels. The fact that that condition existed for a time in the Magnificent was not brought to my attention.
Had that been done, no doubt I would have caused the appropriate officer of the navy to give instructions to destroy the cockroaches, but I think it is somebody else's job to look after cockroaches. I certainly would have expected that the officers of the Magnificent, if that condition existed, would have been competent to deal with it without its having to be reported to me. Quite a few of the other complaints and grievances are of a rather similar character. Put together they present a certain picture, but from my own service experience in the army, if our unit had been interviewed at length in the sympathetic fashion that the officers and men of the Canadian navy were interviewed, you would have had a picture of a most disastrous and appalling situation, whereas I venture to say our unit was one of the best in the Canadian army. Therefore I think it is necessary in considering the report to take into account the fact that the members of the committee making the inquiry were asked to do just this kind of job so that all of us would see the whole picture.
As to recruiting, which is dealt with at page 43, the leader of the opposition (Mr. 1412	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Claxton Drew) followed the members of the committee of inquiry in referring to "soft soap operas". Here again I must say I am not going to enter the lists on the side either of the committee or of the leader of the opposition on the question of the appreciation of the value of advertising of any type. It is a matter on which everybody has an opinion, and one opinion is frequently as good as another. I can speak, however, about recruiting advertising from one point of view, and that is that it produced results. The fact that the navy is the first of the three services to be up to its present establishment in men is striking evidence that the navy got the men it needed, and is continuing to get them. At the present time we have a waiting list for enlistment in certain classes of the navy. We are going to continue to recruit men even if the present establishment is maintained, because there is a wastage of about sixty-six men per month.
Not only did we get the men, but before and during the inquiry we also conducted investigations to see how the men were liking the life. I have talked with a good many of them myself and these investigations, made by people in the services and outside, have shown that by and large the recruits we have been getting for the armed forces have said, after they have been in service for a matter of some weeks or months, that generally speaking they have found conditions of life much better than they expected, indicating that we are not painting too bright a picture of world cruises and the like.
In the light of the report, I have looked again at all the navy advertisements in the last week, and have gone over them in detail.
I can assure hon. members that there is very little in the way of advertising of "world cruises'" indicating that it is going to be a "pleasant episode". The advertising has been aimed at young Canadian boys and men from the age of seventeen up who want a career of usefulness and service to their country where there will be opportunities for them. That is the note that has been emphasized. That is the appeal that has been made, and the fact that the response has been good indicates that we have not been shooting wide of the mark.
I have also compared our advertisements with those of other services, those of other countries, and those of the R.C.M.P., to which reference was made. I must say that from my examination of our advertisements I feel they are suitable for the job, well framed and fair, that they have painted an honest picture, and have obtained results.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister indicate how much money that recruiting has cost?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would have to get the figure for the hon. member. Reference was made at page 60 of the report to the fact that we did not provide laundry facilities at Esquimalt. That is an important thing, but I would not have thought it would warrant particular attention at this time in a budget debate. I have looked into that matter, and I find that, whereas laundry facilities are provided for officers and men of the armed forces at most places, at Esquimalt provision was made in the service's program for last year or the year before, and before it reached me it was taken out by officers of the service on the ground that there were other things which had a greater priority. That is one of the recommendations which depends on treasury action, and which I think should be carried out. I am sure if it had been brought to my attention earlier I would have seen that it was carried out.
With regard to recreational facilities, to which the leader of the opposition referred, quoting from page 70 of the report, I have not seen the building that the members of the committee of inquiry visited at Seattle, but I have seen the recreational building in
H.	M.C.S. Stadacona at Halifax. I know of no better recreational building in any service in any part of Canada. I think it is the equal of anything I have seen in any university with the possible exception of Hart House. I have never seen anything to better it in a Y.M.C.A. or community hall. That is the situation at Halifax. If the building at Seattle is better, then it must be a very fine place, and rather like a good club with all kinds of specialized equipment. The building at Halifax has a swimming pool, a track, a large drill hall floor for badminton and other games and for dances, bowling alleys, billiard tables, ping pong tables, and two rooms containing a large library and a very large record library of serious and jazz music. Altogether it provides a good place for men to seek their quite proper entertainment and recreation.
At Esquimalt we hope to construct a similar building, but there again it is a question of priority. During the last two and a half years I have put the emphasis, so far as our construction program is concerned, on the building of married quarters. I felt that came first, that the one essential thing we needed to do was to enable the officers and men of the armed forces to be united with the members of their families in their own homes in good communities. To that end we started a building program, and have increased the number of married quarters from what it was at the beginning of 1947,
I,	100, to a total of 7,400 or 7,500 when the present year's program is completed. Each

of those quarters relieves the situation with respect to civilian housing, because it enables a service family to make room for a civilian family. We put that first and this program of constructing married quarters has been much bigger, in proportion to the size of our armed forces, than anything I know of being done in any other country. We felt that was needed, because we wanted to create conditions for a good life for our men, particularly our married men, particularly veterans, and more particularly those who had been separated from their families for some time.
The next priority we considered was the building of barrack accommodation to replace some of the barracks that were in bad condition. Two of the worst in the armed forces were those at Halifax and Esquimalt. We have done work on the building at Halifax, and I hope the appropriation for next year will permit us to do what must be done at Esquimalt. This kind of consideration is a question of priority. This year, in the services and through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, we have some $90 million available for the construction, maintenance and repair of buildings. That represents an enormous construction program. When we shall have met the need for married quarters and for more barrack accommodation, undoubtedly we can move forward with regard to recreation; and that will enter into the long-term program.
Then the hon. member mentioned films. The arrangement in all three services is that films are provided to service units through the canteen or other funds raised by the men themselves. It has not been the practice at our ordinary service centres to provide films out of public funds. I think hon. members will agree that this seems reasonable in view of the fact that the men themselves have to pay if they want to see films. But in all three services arrangements are made for the circulation of good films obtained from the agencies on a hire basis. The film society in the navy, which is a voluntary organization, apparently has not been as active as it might have been, and at the time of the incidents I understand Magnificent was not taking films from the film society. At the present time it is, however; so is Ontario, and so are most of the other principal units in the navy. That is largely a matter of internal management, and we will see that greater facilities are provided for securing co-operation in this respect and also for making available more films of the film board and other serious films. However, that is not a very great matter.
The Budget-Mr. Claxton
Then the hon. member referred to Operation Eagle, which I think perhaps I should deal with again when the estimates of the department are under consideration. However, I venture to say that no word of criticism has been or could be uttered about that operation from the point of view of the performance, the ability and the state of training of the officers and men of the P.P.C.L.I. In the second place I do not think a word of criticism has been offered or could be offered about the skill and state of training of the officers and men of the air force, either regular or auxiliary. In the third place I do not think anything has been said or could be said in criticism of the work done by the staffs who planned and carried out the exercise. I make these statements believing, from my discussion with people who were there, either press or otherwise, that they are in accordance with the facts. It was those three things the exercise was designed to test, and the reports by my officers indicate that in these respects the exercise was very successful indeed.
As for equipment, of course the reports did not indicate to us anything we did not know. We have no packet aircraft, and I do not think any country in the world has them except the United States. They are still being modified, and they cost well over half a million dollars each. In this exercise we did use some seventy-two aircraft of a type suitable for the purpose. We did not use any Vampires because it was not an exercise in which we were using Vampires; and to criticize the exercise for not using Vampires or not having one type of equipment or another seems to me about as relevant as criticizing a rifle shoot out at the Connaught rifle ranges because we were not using 5-5 guns. This exercise was planned as a battalion exercise, to test co-operation between the men of the battalion who were doing a parachute jump, and air force units. It produced some very interesting results, which will be profitable in future training.
The exercise was criticized on the ground that the parachutes were patched. There are no patches in the parachutes. In the Canadian forces, as in the United States, if on examination-and parachutes are examined after each use-a parachute is found to have any sign of wear or scuffing of any kind, an entire panel is replaced by a new panel. It happens that the new panels in this case were white and therefore showed up, since the other panels were camouflaged. Apparently this caused someone to say that the parachutes were in bad repair, or were patched.

The Budget-Mr. Claxton

speechtext: I never heard that complaint and never saw it in the newspapers. That report was never brought to my attention; therefore I am not in a position to say whether or not it was justified. It is a new point, which I shall look into. I did see some suggestion that we were to blame because the guns lacked ammunition. I should point out that the guns were firing blanks, and the only effect of any lack in the blanks available at any point would be that the noise would not be as loud as otherwise. However, there is no shortage of blank ammunition in Canada, nor was there any shortage at the scene of the exercise. Some of the reports indicated that the guns had jammed, and that is quite true. The Vickers gun is equipped with a special lock for firing blanks. This lock is not as well machined as the gun itself and sometimes it jams. When it does the soldier clears it. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There were no Ross rifles. I do not want to spend more time on this subject now. The hon. leader of the opposition closed his speech with a reference to the reports of a number of other committees, stating that all those reports had been useful. He mentioned them in support of his plea that there should be a committee of this house on defence. He referred to the Esher


committee of 1904. I might point out that was not a parliamentary committee. The leader of the opposition referred also to the Otter report; that was not a parliamentary committee. He referred to the excellent work done by the council of defence associations, which is not a parliamentary committee. The fact is there has not been a parliamentary committee on defence which made a report, either in the parliament at Westminster or in this parliament. It has not been considered, by any government at any time, that that was a desirable way of doing it.
Now, that is not my decision. It is the view of the government. It has been the view of all governments up until now. I indicated the reasons for it during the discussion of a motion by the member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming) for the appointment of a committee on social security. The reasons are the same, and they are general. So far as I am concerned, I would welcome a committee on defence or anything else, but I do not believe that is the proper method of conducting business in parliament or of running the defence forces of this country. I believe experience in other places supports that view.
The leader of the opposition on this and other occasions gave the impression that the members of the opposition had consistently been refused information about the defence forces and defence matters. That statement would paint a picture of requests coming from members of the opposition almost daily. 1 should tell this house that, so far as I know, I have never received a private request from any member of any of the opposition groups that I have not answered. With regard to questions put in the house-I have not had an opportunity of checking my own records or those of the department because I have been in the house ever since the leader of the opposition raised the point-I believe I am right in saying that only one request for information has been refused in the last year and a half, and that was made by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness). It was refused on the advice of my advisers, after the most serious consideration, for reasons which were made clear at the time. It is not the practice and has not been the practice, in this or any other country which has the parliamentary system of government and particularly at Westminster, to give specific information about the strength or the trained strength of the units of the active forces.
The reason for that has been made plain on a number of occasions. 1 believe that reason has appealed to the good sense of the majority of hon. members as well as to the people throughout the country. So far as I am aware that is the only bit of information, certainly

it is the only type of information, that has been the subject of an inquiry that has met with such a reply.
The leader of the opposition said they would be failing in their duty if they did not have an opportunity of making an examination of the over-all plan, the suitability of the forces, effectiveness of training, and the proper expenditure of money. It seems to me those are all proper matters for discussion at any length, and in any detail, in the consideration of the estimates of this department. That is the type of matter which has been discussed when the defence estimates have come before this house on previous occasions. I shall welcome a discussion of them to the fullest possible extent when the estimates of the department come before this house, which I hope will be at an early date. I hope we can have then a debate on defence matters. I shall be glad indeed to give every possible bit of information about anything relative to the work, aims or objects of the defence forces that we do not believe is contrary to the national interest. So far as I am aware, that has been limited in the past only in the way I have indicated.
It seems to me that the best time to take all this up is on the defence estimates rather than on the budget. Certainly I did not come here today expecting to make this speech. In conclusion, I should like to say that I have been in this portfolio for two and a half years. In that time, I have met most of the officers and many of the men in the armed forces in Canada; I have visited the units, active and reserve, and I have been proud to be associated with them in this work. It has been a work full of interest and full of difficulties, as is indicated by the subject matter of this report as well as by events in other countries. It is a work in which we can show results, and there are signs which give encouragement.
With regard to organization, I believe I can say without fear of successful contradiction that in the work of unification, co-ordination and the streamlining of our forces, navy, army and air forces, the Department of National Defence of Canada has made more progress than any other country in the world. I believe that in the all-important question of the training of officers we have, in the various plans in effect in Canada, subject to such adjustment as we will make particularly in regard to executive officers in the navy, more candidates for commissioned ranks in the three services training to our standards than any country in the world. With regard to the general work and training activities of the armed forces, we are making steady progress. Recruiting for the active forces is proceeding at the rate we want, so that the target for the 45781-90
The Budget-Mr. Rooney army will be met in September and for the air force in December of 1950. With the continued support of the members of this honourable house and the constructive, useful criticism of the loyal and all other opposition, I believe we shall build up our armed forces in a way which will redound to the credit and security of Canada.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the record may I add my congratulations to those which have been extended to you by hon. members. I have always felt that in your appointment it was a friend appointed. It must be apparent to all that you are carrying out the duties of your high office with dignity and all fairness.
I also desire to congratulate the mover (Mr. Boisvert) and the seconder (Mr. Laing) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne As a newcomer to the house I was told by one of my friends to read a certain book written by George W. Ross entitled "In and Out of Parliament" in which he said that you should get up as soon as you can, because if you are going to get thrown out of the house you may as well get thrown out early.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I had a wonderful apple presented to me. Some time ago we had peaches and other fruit presented to us. I sent to St. Paul's in Toronto to see if we had apples or any other fruit. After they had made their report the consensus was that we had only one apple tree and they could find only a couple of apples on it. But in St. Paul's, when you visit there, what we can give you is hospitality and good will. When you visit Toronto, whether you come by rail or water, you will land in St. Paul's riding, the very centre of the capital of the banner province of all Canada, which I have the great honour to represent.
It was with a feeling of pride in our government that I listened to the terms of the budget which was presented to the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Throughout the years of the war and in the years prior to and since the war the Liberal government has built up a consistent record of wise and honest administration, which I maintain is again reflected in the present budget. Under the long and brilliant leadership of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Canada has grown and prospered and has become one of the major nations of the world today. I suggest, sir, that under the leadership of

The Budget-Mr. Rooney the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the torch will be carried high and his name will go down in history along with King, Laurier and Macdonald as one of the greatest leaders since confederation.
In the time at my disposal tonight I propose to direct my remarks to that portion of the budget relating to housing, in this sense, that the federal government, as well as rendering financial aid in one form or another, should also give serious consideration to the location and type of future housing projects which more and more are becoming allimportant factors in our national housing problem. Relief for our people in the matter of housing has been, and still is, one of the most pressing needs. It is one to which the federal government, through its crown company, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, under the capable direction of Mr. D. B. Mansur, has extended all possible ud in money and materials in an effort to speed up construction of homes for the people. In spite of this, the scarcity of dwellings, or living accommodation of any kind, within the means of the average person, still continues. One needs only to read local newspapers to realize the situation.
I am sure we all agree with the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) that the housing shortage, which started during wartime and continued into the post-war years, gives every promise of becoming a longterm peacetime problem. Therefore, any approach to the problem should be made with that end in view, and will require the joint efforts of the three levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal, together with private endeavours.
Methods used to solve an extreme housing shortage during periods of emergency cannot be applied with the same success when the need remains continuous for a lengthy time, and will only bring further additional problems.	,
Up to the present, for the most part, we have largely attempted to meet the situation by the building of small dwellings on the outskirts of our towns and cities where land was readily available for the purpose. If we continue to solve our problem in this manner when we are faced with a long-term housing shortage, will it not have the effect of creating additional problems, such as transportation, schools, roadways, sewers, and water for communities already overburdened with taxation, and will it solve the dwelling needs of the majority of citizens? I personally do not think so as the large percentage of those citizens belong to that vast group of workers who must go forth daily to their work, individuals and married couples where both husband and wife must work. Housing units for


this class of citizen should, therefore, be located within easy distance of their work. In any city or large town, I believe it will be found that the greatest number of persons are employed in the downtown section of the community. This is why in our cities and towns we find people living in deplorable conditions in overcrowded rooming houses or in run-down small houses in our so-called slum areas of our downtown sections. The only remedy offered these people in the matter of improved conditions is a single family unit miles away from their work on the outskirts of the city, which in most cases would be out of the question financially, even with assistance, and in addition most of them do not require or want a house.
As a resident of the city of Toronto, I have recently made a partial survey of conditions in that area as they relate to housing, particularly in St. Paul's riding, which I have the honour to represent. To illustrate my point I would like to briefly outline some of my findings.
Toronto is the second largest city in Canada, covering an area slightly over forty square miles, with a population of 670,000. The assessed value of its taxable property is $1,172,000,000. St. Paul's riding, covering an area of almost five square miles, cuts through the centre of the city from the Toronto harbour on the south almost to Eglinton avenue on the north, a distance of four and a half miles. It has a population of 72,347 and the assessed value of its taxable property is $356,694,000-30-43 per cent of all the assessed property value in the entire city. This may be a reason why St. Paul's is called the richest riding in Canada.
Within the southerly area of St. Paul's is located the heart of Toronto's financial district, with its skyscrapers and many large office buildings, its docks and warehouses, and a large percentage of the city's hotels, theatres, hospitals, government buildings, and business establishments, some of which are: the union station, the dominion public building, the postal terminal, the harbour commission building, the Royal York hotel, the King Edward hotel; the head office in Ontario of the Bank of Montreal, which has just moved into its $8 million buildings, and the Royal Bank of Canada; the head offices of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, the tallest building in the British empire, the Bank of Nova Scotia's new building under construction, the Imperial Bank of Canada, the Bank of Toronto and the Dominion Bank; the head offices of the Canada Permanent Trust Company, the Toronto General Trusts Corporation, the National Trust Company, the Chartered Trust and Executor Company; the head offices of

the Canada Life Assurance Company, the Confederation Life Association, the British American Life Assurance Company; the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Bell Telephone Company of Canada; the three daily newspaper offices and plants-the Toronto Daily Star, the Globe and Mail and the Telegram-the Metropolitan building, the National building, the university of Toronto buildings, the Royal Ontario museum; the two great department stores, the T. Eaton Company and the Robert Simpson Company; Maple Leaf Gardens, St. Michael's hospital, the Toronto General hospital, the Women's hospital, the Wellesley hospital, the Mount Sinai hospital, the Hospital for Sick Children now under construction.
From the foregoing list of large companies and institutions one can readily see the vast number of persons who would be required to staff them. For example the two largest departmental stores employ a combined total of 21,850 people. At Christmastime there is an additional 8,000, making roughly 30,000 people working in these two stores. In addition there are countless other large and small businesses and factories too numerous to mention. In passing I might say that the university of Toronto has 3,000 employees, with 13,700 students.
In all there are literally tens of thousands of workers employed in the downtown section of St. Paul's riding. This fact is borne out by the following figures received from the Toronto transportation commission. The commission carries in the city of Toronto approximately 960,000 people in the normal week day, of which number a total of 240,000 people are carried daily into the downtown section of St. Paul's riding.
In other words, one-quarter of what they carry in the city of Toronto is carried daily into St. Paul's riding, which I have the honour to represent. Unfortunately the residential areas surrounding this downtown business district have never undergone any change in the way of remodelling or rebuilding in order to meet the ever-growing demand caused by the ever-increasing number of persons employed in that section. The many city blocks of residences, large and small, in the central, east and west sections of my riding were all built years and years ago. They are long since obsolete even for the purpose for which they were built, let alone for the purposes for which they are now being used, which are rooming houses for the large ones, and families too large for the small ones. In addition, there are row after row of old stores, with one or two storeys over them which are used for dwelling accommodation, and which are in many cases actually unfit for living in or for any other use.
