subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising this evening is to deal exclusively with three or four matters which
The Budget-Mr. Shaw have been alluded to during the course of this budget debate. Were it not for the fact that certain rather fallacious arguments have been advanced, arguments bolstered by deceptive evidence resulting in wholly erroneous conclusions, I probably would not find it necessary to participate in the discussion at this time.
The first matter to which I should like to refer has to do with oil. Perhaps this could be designated more properly as the farmer in relation to oil, or still more properly as mineral rights in relation to the farmers of my province of Alberta. At least two assertions have been made during the course of this debate which may well leave the impression that farmers living in the province of Alberta are, as a consequence of the policies of the government of that province, being deprived of all but, as one hon. member said, a smile and not a very pleasant one. I should like to quote from page 1122 of Hansard of October 25, 1949. Speaking at that time the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) made this assertion:
The other day a few hundred acres of land in Alberta were sold to one of the oil companies for over $3 million cold cash for just the right to search. No oil had yet been found there. What did the farmer who owned the land get? A smile, and not a very pleasant one.
In the first place no land was sold to any oil company. The company only purchased drilling rights. Secondly, I emphasize what he said, namely, that no oil had yet been found. This is the speech in which the hon. member for Athabaska made an earnest plea for the completion of a certain line of railroad in northern Alberta. In that connection the hon. member for Athabaska has our whole-hearted support. This is the speech in which the hon. member assailed the Conservative government under the late R. B. Bennett for having discontinued operations on that line during the first five years of the depression. After assailing the government of that period he said that then the war came. This is the speech in which he forgot to mention that there were four years and some months of depression between the defeat of the Conservative government and the outbreak of the war with a Liberal government in office, and nothing was done to hasten the completion of that railroad. I mention that simply because he forgot to- or did he?
I should also like to quote from Hansard of November 1, 1949, page 1329. In this instance the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) was speaking, and he said:
The farmers upon whose land oil is discovered receive little direct benefit from the discovery because few of them have mineral rights. All that

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
these farmers receive is the rancid smell of oil twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, plus a little compensation for the use of their land.
I suggest to the hon. member lor Athabaska and the hon. member for Vegreville that they ought to hold a caucus and endeavour to come to some agreement with respect to what the farmer in Alberta does or does not get because in one instance the hon. member for Athabaska said he got nothing but a smile, and not a very pleasant one at that, and in the other instance the hon. member for Vegreville said he got some slight compensation, including the rancid smell of oil. I will show that they are both wrong.
What are the facts, Mr. Speaker? After all, facts mean far more than the imaginary wanderings of some minds. When the resources were returned to the province of Alberta in the early thirties, 51 per cent of such resources had already been alienated by the government of Canada. Therefore the province of Alberta only had 49 per cent to deal with. The government of the province of Alberta owns the mineral rights on considerable land in the province. That is a fact. It is also a fact that certain farmers own mineral rights on their lands in the province. On lands where the province owns the mineral rights, drilling rights are sold to oil companies. Tenders are called for and bids considered. It is a fact that millions of dollars have gone into the public treasury of the province as a consequence of the sale of these rights. The company drills, and if it strikes oil 12| per cent of all production goes into the treasury of the province of Alberta. To be used for what purpose? To be used for the welfare of all the people of the province of Alberta to build roads, to provide better and more extensive health services, to provide educational services, for debt reduction, tax reduction, and also for other purposes.
Where does the farmer stand who does not own the mineral rights? Is it true that he gets nothing but a smile, and not a pleasant one, or very limited compensation? I wish to refer to some of the facts as they are found in an official publication of the government of the province, entitled "Surface Rights". The part to which I wish to refer reads:
Under the common law which was in force for many years in Alberta, as well as other provinces of the dominion, the title to mines and minerals always included the right of entry and reasonable use of the surface for the purpose of working the minerals, including oil and gas. The owner of minerals had a vested right to use as much of the surface as might be required for his operations without any compensation to the surface owner or without liability except for negligence. In carrying out a program of oil development, which is so necessary in any country, provision must be made in the public interest whereby those engaged in the

development might enter upon the land where development work is to be undertaken. However, the government-
Referring to the government of the province of Alberta.
-is convinced that the owner of the surface is entitled to full compensation as he would be in case a canal, a railway, a highway, a power line, a coal mine or any other thing required in the public interest would cause him any damage or inconvenience.
In 1947, Mr. Speaker, an act known as the Right of Entry Arbitration Act was passed which provided for the setting up of a board of arbitration in the province of Alberta with wide powers to deal with the matter of compensation to surface owners. What factors are taken into consideration by that board? They are, first, the value of the land; second, the amount of land which may be permanently damaged by the operator's operations; third, the adverse effect of the right of entry on the remaining land; fourth, compensation for severance; fifth, compensation for the nuisance, inconvenience and noise which may be caused by or arise from or in connection with the operations; and finally such other factors as the board may from time to time deem proper, relevant or applicable.
This legislation shows one thing. It demonstrates the intention and desire of the government of Alberta to give the board of arbitration all necessary leeway to deal with applications from the standpoint of equity and justice. Let me cite five cases that were dealt with by the board of arbitration in order that we may see whether the farmer gets just a smile, and not a very pleasant one, or something comparable. This is the first case: payment for one well, $1,188, plus annual compensation of $420 for the life of the well. Case No. 2: $1,288 as the first payment, and $428.50 every year thereafter for the life of the well. Case No. 3: $1,551 as the first payment, and $461 every year thereafter, in each case for one well. Case No. 4: $1,400, with $500 payable every year thereafter for the life of the well. Case No. 5: $2,000 the first year, with $700 per year thereafter for the entire life of the well. From the information I have given it will be readily seen that from a quarter section of land on which four wells are drilled-and that is not at all uncommon- the farmer would receive an average of approximately $6,000 the first year and $2,000 for every year the wells operate, which might be twenty years. The farmer also enjoys the right to continue to farm his land during that time. After all, once a well is brought in, very little of the farm is taken out of production. As the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) says, it amounts to only a few

square feet. And I must emphasize that these are cases in which the farmer does not hold the mineral rights.
Further in his speech the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) advocated that all farmers on whose land oil is found should be paid royalties. I think the Calgary Albertan, which supported the Liberal party with all its vigour during the last campaign, dealt more effectively than I could with that suggestion. I refer to an editorial under date of October 28 of this year, under the heading, "Don't Pension a Few Northern Farmers." The editorial states:
It is unfortunate that a man of the stature of Mr. J. M. Dechene. Liberal M.P. for Athabaska in northern Alberta, should be so far off the beam on this matter of oil royalties. In parliament, the other day, he said the oil belonged "to the people, not to the provincial government,'' and the provincial government should give a big slice of its royalty income (he suggested 5 of the 121 per cent) to the farmer under whose land the oil was found. He wanted something done "to see that the farmer out of whose land this wealth is taken receives a royalty."
Except on C.P.R., Hudson's Bay and certain other freehold land, the great bulk of the oil is owned by the provincial government, which is all the people of Alberta. The farmer who owns the surface has no more right to the oil under his land than the farmer who lives three hundred miles away. It is not his. It belongs to the government and thus to all the people. If the government gives him a slice of its 121 per cent royalty it is depriving all the other rightful owners of their just income. It is robbing 99-9 per cent of the farmers to give a modest and entirely undeserved fortune to -1 per cent of the farmers.
The only way that the real owners, meaning all the citizens of Alberta, can benefit from their ownership is through the provincial government. It is taking many millions of dollars a year out of the oil industry, and rightly so. That money can be used to permit the reduction of taxes, which we strongly oppose. Or it can be used first to pay off the provincial debt and then to build roads, schools, hospitals and other capital assets which all the people of Alberta could enjoy. That use of the oil money we strongly support. But never, never should the province use its royalty to pension off a few farmers in Mr. Dechene's constituency, who have no more right to it than anybody else in the province.
I think that editorial is rather significant. I must add that the Liberals in Alberta are finding it desperately difficult to make election issues. Why, they even grabbed this, which the C.C.F. leader could not drop soon enough after he had picked it up the first time. The Liberals are using this and endeavouring to make capital out of it. The other day that same newspaper, the Albertan, dealt with the Liberal leader in Alberta and his criticism of oil policy. First it deflated him editorially; after deflating him it dissected his arguments, and then exposed them to the ridicule of the public of that province. That was how it dealt with Mr. Harper Prowse, leader of the Liberals in the province of Alberta.
The Budget-Mr. Shaw
The government of my province believes that in dealing with this most important question sense, reason, good judgment and good business practices are the things that count. Obviously to the Liberals of that province these things, at any rate in relation to oil, have all gone with the wind. Before leaving this matter I want to refer to another editorial, which also appeared in the Albertan. I am always pleased to be able to quote that newspaper to Liberals, because I cannot forget how strongly it supported them during the last campaign. An editorial under date of October 25, referring to Liberalism and oil, had this to say in part:
It was during the Borden administration, when the Alberta government was Liberal and so was the Senate. The Alberta government, it seems, wanted to give the Shell Oil Company exclusive oil rights for the whole province in return for a payment of $5,000. But it didn't have the power to do so, so it asked the federal government to give it that power. The enabling legislation went through the commons but the Senate turned it down.
So, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to condemning whatever may be done in the province of Alberta in connection with oil, such condemnation should not be voiced by the Liberals.
Now I come to matter No. 2. The day before yesterday, November 1, a certain textbook was brought into this house. I did not see the book, but I know all about it. It is called "The World of Today", by Paterson and McDougall, and has been used in the province of Alberta. Incidentally, this matter is not new in the House of Commons. It was brought into this house over eight and a half years ago by the hon. member for Athabaska, who used almost the same arguments that were used the day before yesterday and drew the same fallacious conclusions. Eight and a half years ago, Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Lethbridge took these arguments and buried them about six feet deep under logic and truth. Now, eight and a half years later the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Decore), in a ipolitically ghoulish fashion, exhumes the bones of that argument and makes an effort to cloak them with the same arguments that killed the thing eight and a half years ago, leaving the same type of impression-at least, first he tried to breathe life into the thing and failed miserably.

All right, I will deal with it. I am going to deal with it not from the standpoint of what he said, but from the standpoint of what he did not say, which is often more important. He did not tell this house that Mr. Paterson was the editor of the Ryer-son Press in Toronto, or that Mr. McDougall

The Budget-Mr. Shaw was principal of the normal practice school in Edmonton. No, he wanted to leave the impression that the writers were probably members of the Alberta government. He did not inform this house, and I ask my friends to listen, that Saskatchewan, under a Liberal government and with a Liberal minister of education, used the same textbooks for years. He did not indicate that, Mr. Speaker. Undoubtedly, he did not know-or did he?
This is significant. At page 1329 of Hansard, after referring to this book, he quoted the following from it:
Some people feel-
Notice that.
Some people feel that the capitalist (competitive) system is out of date in this modern world, and should be modified or replaced entirely by a system better fitted to deal with the problems of today. Three of these plans are especially interesting: The Communist (as in Russia), the C.C.F., and Social Credit.
He referred to this book after saying he did not mind having his children learn about these different things, but that it was vicious propaganda. I would ask my hon. friend if it is not a fact that some people do feel, as it says here, that there are alternatives to the capitalist or competitive system. You have heard that said in this house. I cannot see anything vicious in that. Like my hon. friend, I taught school for many years. I tried to give my pupils both sides of the question. I told them there are some people who believe there are alternatives to the capitalist system. I gave them the truth, the whole truth, and let them form their own opinions. What he did not seem to know, Mr. Speaker, or it would have wrecked his whole argument, is that Social Crediters have not advocated the implementation of a system to take the place of the capitalist or competitive system, if you want to call it that. Let him remember that. I repeat that he does not seem to realize that there are two sides to every question, not only here but in all events of our everyday life. I am not so sure that I would want him to teach my children if he were going to deal with only that one side of each question.
Reference was also made, Mr. Speaker, to education. No group in this House of Commons has taken a firmer stand than we have in support of federal grants in aid to assist the provinces in establishing equality of opportunity in the field of education. Let me make that quite clear. The hon. member for Vegre-ville said at page 1329 of Hansard:
In our province of Alberta there is no earthly excuse for the government not making more substantial grants to education which would be in keeping with the requirements and the expanding needs in that province.
Obviously, in making that statement, the member for Vegreville was not aware of one
[Mr. Shaw.}

or two things. First, from the fiscal year 1934-35 to 1948-49, educational grants in the province of Alberta increased from $2,269,286.41 to $9,829,000. In other words, our assistance to education has increased much more rapidly than has the income of the province of Alberta. In order to assist in the equalization of educational opportunity in my province, the government, in many districts, is paying as high as eighty-five per cent of the cost of education. Those are the more remote, less prosperous areas. That is one effective method of bringing about equalization of educational opportunity.
We realize, Mr. Speaker, and admit that the revenues of our province have increased quite rapidly during these past few years. But we believe in facing the situation realistically. We are not unmindful of the fact that the present government of Alberta took over the affairs of the province in 1935. At that time we had $158 million of debt; $95 million of it given by the Liberal government between 1905 and 1921. It is that period which the Bank of Canada characterized in its 1937 report as the period of waste, extravagance and loose administration. The farmer government of that province gave us another $63 million in debt. Of course, $51 million of our total debt accumulated as a consequence of the depression-a depression which we feel justified in attributing, at least in part, to some of the asinine financial policies of the dominion government.
The government of the province of Alberta realizes what a good many Liberals do not seem to realize, namely, that the gas and oil resources are a wasting asset. I think that should be underlined. It is quite conceivable that within forty years the oil and gas fields in my province may be completely depleted. All one has to do is look at what has happened in Turner valley to visualize what could occur in my province, if the government were to heed those who have neither vision nor good business judgment and load the budget with a burden of fixed charges right up to the level of revenues. I ask some of our critics to consider that. If that were done and, after forty or fifty years, the revenues were down or falling materially, it would leave the province with that burden of fixed charges and nothing with which to pay them. The government of Alberta wisely takes the stand that a portion of the present income from gas and oil must be used to create other assets which will be well enough developed at the end of forty years to enable the services of the province to be carried on uninterrupted. With the depletion of these oil and gas fields the revenues would go, Mr. Speaker. That, I contend, in the field

of provincial or any other administration, is nothing but vision and good business practice.
We have heard in this house, in the province of Alberta, and from the Liberal leader and his followers, that we should pile up a burden of fixed charges by utilizing the resources which we have now in their entirety for current activities within that province. Well, I say to you that we contend vision has been displayed in dealing with the matter. We have increased the grants to education in the province by almost five times. We still say, however,-and this is in keeping with part of my hon. friend's remarks-that we must have federal grants in aid in order to assist in the equalization of educational opportunity across this country.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer, Mr. Speaker. In a speech on Tuesday, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) made reference to something which I had said previously in the House of Commons, as reported at page 1330 of Hansard. I would not refer to it at all of course if it were not almost laughable. I quote:
However, I have heard of expressions coming from some of my Social Credit friends-and when I say some of them, I mean just some of them-
Of course he should have named me.
-to the effect that my election to this house was made possible by the communist vote of the Vegreville constituency, and I intend to deal with this matter. The insinuations are quite clear. Mr. Speaker.
I interject here to say that he is wrong. There were no insinuations. I made cold, blunt, hard statements that were true. There were no insinuations. I continue with the quotation:
Such statements cast a reflection not only on the nine thousand people who voted for me in the election of June 27 but also on all the people in that constituency, numbering some 60,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, you notice what he has endeavoured to do. He has endeavoured to take my assertions and portray them as a reflection upon the 60,000 people in his riding. Out west we call that buncombe. He did not take the figures which I gave in this house in my last speech and endeavour to break them down or destroy them at all. I know that Vegreville constituency. I know that it embraces a fine part of the province of Alberta. I know its people. Thousands of these people are good citizens, energetic, sincere, honest, one hundred per cent Canadians. The hon. member's statement to the press on October 6 to the contrary notwithstanding, I know these things from personal experience.
Notwithstanding the fact that the great majority of these people are as I have described them, there are, and he cannot deny it, between three thousand and four thousand
The Budget-Mr. Shaw communists within his riding. And whether these communists are of Anglo-Saxon, French or Ukrainian origin, they are still communists. They are traitors to democracy and traitors to the democratic concept of human organization. The hon. member did not in any way, shape or form refute the concrete evidence which I put on the record, Mr. Speaker.
I hold in my hand a circular which was circulated by the thousands in the Vegreville constituency during the last election. This circular is headed:
Voters of Vegreville Constituency!
On election day, June 27, you will need to make a choice. On that day you will be marking your ballot for the man you want to represent you in the House of Commons for the next four years. You will be judged throughout the country by the man you choose.
After a vicious attack upon the former member for Vegreville, Mr. Hlynka, they went on to say:
The Labour-Progressive party calls on the people of Vegreville to defeat Anthony Hlynka on June 27. Vote against him! Put him out of office! Send this war-mongering, pro-fascist back where he belongs!
Then they go on to show that they have no love whatsoever for the Liberal party. They say:
The Labour-Progressive party is campaigning in every constituency for peace, democracy and security. In Vegreville constituency we decided not to nominate a candidate in this election. We decided this because we do not want to split democratic opinion in the constituency as then Hlynka might get back in. We say to all voters in Vegreville: Stand united! Vote united! Defeat your main enemy-Hlynka.
We greet the decision of the C.C.F. to also not contest this constituency. We urge all C.C.F. supporters to actively campaign against Hlynka and to help defeat him.
Go to the polls on Monday, June 27, and vote against Hlynka!
There were and there are between three and four thousand communist supporters-

In the early days of our movement, that is in its infancy, it is conceivable that a few communists may have wormed their way in, but it did not take any more than a good political delousing to get rid of them. What the Liberal party needs in certain parts of its organization today is a complete political delousing to get rid of the communists. They can make their insinuations on the floor of the House of Commons, but I ask any Liberal in this house if he can produce evidence of propaganda published by the Social Credit party containing the pictures of communist leaders. I have in front of me propaganda published and distributed within the last six years under the authority of the Liberal association containing the pictures of some of Canada's outstanding communists. That occurred within recent times. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, we say that at least in certain quarters of the Liberal party a good political delousing would do them a lot of good in order to get rid of the communists, who are still within certain sections of that organization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his remarks on Friday, October 26, as recorded at page 1223 of Hansard, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated that hon. members interested in the subject of education could discuss it in this debate. I am going to follow his suggestion, and shall take a rather unusual line for one who is not a member of the government party. I suspect that much of what I shall say tonight will be


used against me at some future time in York South. Nevertheless I am interested in education in Canada, and in order to lay that ghost of suspicion which is abroad, that the federal government dare not touch education without stepping on provincial corns, I propose tonight briefly to review the extent to which the federal government is involved in educational work at the present time.
First of all, I am sorry the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) is not in the house. It is not often I can compliment him; but I wish to pay tribute to him and to his assistants for the good educational work carried on by the Department of Labour under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act of 1942. The minister and his assistants deserve high commendation for their administration of that act, and particularly I suggest for the great measure of co-operation with the provincial departments of education they have been able to develop and maintain.
The vocational training branch of the Department of Labour from 1937 to March 10, 1948, has had an enrolment of approximately 918,000 students, young and old, and during that period has spent approximately $65 million of federal money on vocational education in Canada at the secondary school and university level. That money has been spent to assist students at the universities, to assist unemployed youth training in the country, to provide courses in forestry, to provide vocational training for the armed forces during the war, training for war industry during the war, pre-matriculation and vocational courses for veterans, apprenticeship training and training or re-training of older unemployed.
All this educational work, even that for which the federal government itself was directly responsible, has been carried on in the very closest co-operation with the provincial departments of education. I note in the Canadian vocational training report that an agreement known as the vocational schools assistance agreement was made with the provinces in 1945, and that it provides, first, an outright annual grant of $10,000 to each province; second, an annual grant of $1,910,000 for a ten-year period to be allotted among the provinces; and, third, a dominion contribution of $10 million to be allotted among the provinces for capital expenditures on building and equipment for vocational training purposes.
All projects which were to be assisted under that agreement were to be approved by the minister before April 1, 1948. I wish now to quote a paragraph from the vocational training report for the past year, which states: At the meeting of the vocational training advisory council which was held on October 4, 1948, various members drew attention to the fact that increased

costs for new buildings and higher operational costs of vocational schools, have reduced the value of the grants which were provided under the vocational schools assistance agreement.
The availability of dominion funds has given a notable impetus to vocational education in Canada, and has been responsible for an active program of development in practically all provinces. Many projects have not been completed, and some have not even been commenced.
The council felt it was in the interests of Canada that facilities for vocational education should be strengthened and developed as speedily as possible. It is recommended that a further grant of S5 million be made by the dominion for capital expenditures, to be distributed on the same basis as the earlier capital grant, and that the annual grants be increased from $2 million to $4 million.
Then the report goes on to say:
As of March 31 these recommendations were still under consideration.
I submit that that recommendation of the advisory council is worth special consideration at this time, and I would urge the Minister of Labour to proceed immediately with the implementation of his council's recommendation. Let me give one example, one with which I am most familiar because it pertains to my own riding of York South.
In York South, with a population of well over 100,000 people, we have three collegiate institutes, but no technical school. Today there are well over a thousand pupils in that riding wanting technical education, but none is available. The school board had planned to build a vocational school which would accommodate a thousand pupils, provided a federal grant is available. Unfortunately they were unable to complete their plans so as to get under the wire by April 1, 1948. In any case I understand the $10 million had all been allotted for approved projects before that. So, without federal assistance, York township will be forced to build a school to accommodate 600 pupils instead of 1,000, a school with one gymnasium instead of two, a school of that size without any auditorium.
This is just one example of many such cases throughout Canada. Unless the government will act and act quickly thousands of young people will be deprived of the opportunity for vocational education. This is not a matter in which we can afford any delay. Young people want education now; they do not want to have to wait three or four years while the government is getting around to the consideration of one of its own council's recommendations.
I pass now from the Department of Labour to the Department of Veterans Affairs in order to show just how deeply the federal government is already involved in education. Up to September 30,	1949, the Department of
Veterans Affairs had assisted 55,260 veterans in under-graduate courses at universities, 6,000 in post-graduate courses, and another 85,900 45781-91A
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy veterans in vocational training at the secondary school level, making a total of 147,160 veterans who have received allowances and tuition from that department.
That is no slight contribution to education on the part of a government which normally is supposed to be keeping out of education entirely. The Department of Veterans Affairs paid $116,685,595 in allowances, over $30 million in tuition fees and nearly $15 million in supplementary grants to universities to compensate the universities for the difference between the payment of fees and the cost of educating these veterans.
I should like to digress for a few moments to say that since coming to this house I have had occasion to refer to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) and his superintendent of educational training, Mr. Jamieson, a considerable number of individual cases. In my opinion both the minister and the superintendent are handicapped by narrow, rigid regulations that I certainly would have opposed to the best of my ability on the floor of this house had I been here when they first came into effect. Nevertheless, I want to add that, subject to those overriding regulations, every single educational case that I have referred to the minister and his superintendent has received the most sympathetic consideration possible. I am pleased to say that in several cases, notwithstanding the limitations of ironclad regulations, ways and means of assisting students have been discovered.
I turn now briefly to the Department of National Defence. I have been unable to put a price tag on the educational work done by that department, but reference to their report for the current fiscal year shows that during last year there were 4,119 army, navy and air force personnel taking undergraduate and post-graduate courses in thirty colleges and universities in Canada and in twelve colleges and universities outside Canada.
I should like to take a few moments of my time to refer to the educational work that was carried on by the Canadian Legion educational services during the war, and is still being carried on by that organization. I have been unable to get any figures to show the extent of their work overseas during the war, but in Canada and Newfoundland during the war years the C.L.E.S. had an enrolment of 215,818 in their correspondence courses and spent $3,130,941. In addition to those correspondence courses, there were nearly half a million members of the armed forces registered in the oral classes that were conducted by the C.L.E.S.
This same organization purchased in Canada for distribution among the forces in Canada

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy and Newfoundland over 3 million library books and carried on 92 courses of study at the matriculation and university levels. One remarkable feature of the work of that organization is the fact that they were able to get the co-operation of the departments of education of all the ten provinces. More than that, every department of education in Canada accepted their certificates of achievement and every university in Canada accepted their senior matriculation certificates for university entrance. I am told that up to the present time there are approximately 11,000 veterans in veterans' institutions, in the federal civil service, and elsewhere who are still taking courses of the Canadian Legion educational services.
Another department involved in educational work is the Department of National Health and Welfare. In 1946 that department appropriated $100,000 for the provision of scholarships and the extension of educational facilities in the seven schools of social work in Canada. For some mysterious reason, I presume known only to that still more mysterious body known as the treasury board, that amount was reduced in 1947-48 to $50,000, and it still stands at that figure. The result is that practically the entire grant has been used for the extension of school facilities and practically none is available for scholarships. I am sure that everyone interested in education in Canada, except possibly the treasury board, is anxious to see that $50,000 raised to the original $100,000 in the next estimates.
The national research council has also given direct aid to education. When that council was set up in 1916 one of the first things it did was to set aside $5,500 of its appropriation for research into medicine and pure science. Over the years that amount has been gradually increased until in 1948 there were 178 scholarships provided by the national research council of a value of $160,150. In addition to that there were grants in aid paid to 17 universities and educational institutions to the value of well over $200,000.
The Department of Trade and Commerce, through the bureau of statistics and especially through the education division of that bureau, has been making its contribution to education. It is true that in the educational field the dominion bureau of statistics unfortunately is limited by its charter to the compilation of educational statistics, but even that in itself is of immense interest to education across Canada. Only in the publications of that branch can we find educational statistics from all the provinces brought together and properly correlated.
I want to repeat the plea that I made in this house over five years ago. It is high time that we had in Canada a federal education

office that would do for Canadian education what the federal office in Washington does for education in that country. I believe that the charter of the education branch of the dominion bureau of statistics should be broadened and that sufficient help should be provided in order that that division may be able to do some of the things that need to be done, things that are either not being done at all or are being done in a haphazard fashion by volunteer organizations.
For instance, there is the whole field of research in education for the benefit of the country at large. It is true that the provinces are carrying on a great deal of educational research, but there is no federal agency in that field. I understand that the Canadian Life Insurance Officers' Association have been spending about $10,000 a year for the past few years in research on school health projects. My information is that that will be discontinued this year. Here is a field of research that will pay national dividends in the future and such a project should not have to rely on private and public campaigns for funds to carry on.
There is another research project being carried on through the -co-operation and support of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the labour congresses. This is a project the purpose of which is to discover to what extent our schools are giving the training best suited to the needs of our communities. If we had a federal bureau of research in education, projects such as these could be carried out for the benefit of the nation, and the research work that is done by the provinces could be correlated and made available for the use of educationists all across the country. We need a federal institution for educational guidance. Most of the schools in the larger centres have educational guidance officers, but educational guidance officers should have a knowledge of, and be able to benefit by, the experience and the data collected by the employment offices all over Canada. Educational guidance today cannot be successfully carried on within the limits of any one province.
We no longer educate boys and girls tc remain citizens of any one province. At least one out of every three students educated in our provinces earns a living in a different province from that in which he or she was born and educated. We need some agency that will compile and keep up to date the vast number of government publications which could be of inestimable value to the schools of the nation if only teachers knew what these publications were, and how and where to get them. These publications, valuable as many of them are, are left to gather dust in some back office or storeroom

just because we have no agency to provide us with a list of the material of that nature that could be made available for use in our schools. There is no list available today of all the educational institutions in Canada. Guidance officers have been asking for such a list. Nowhere today can you get a complete list of all the educational institutions. I suggest that is a job for an office such as the educational branch of the dominion bureau of statistics. It is impossible today to find a list of what scholarships are available. Pupils have a knowledge of the scholarships established by their own schools or their own communities. It is impossible for a student in any one school to know even what scholarships are available within his province. There is no way in which a student can find out what scholarships are available throughout Canada for which he could compete. I suggest that is another job that could be done by the educational branch of the dominion bureau of statistics.
I want to turn for a few moments to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have not time to deal at any length with what I consider to be some of the excellent features of its programs. If I had an hour instead of forty minutes in which to make my speech I could really inform Liberal members of the house of just what a good job the C.B.C. is doing on a very small budget. I want to mention-and again I regret I have not time to develop the subject at any length-the educational work that is being done by the national film board. I want to refer to one paragraph from my prepared speech that has a particular connection with schools. The board maintains a complete visual aid service for schools, including films, film strips, glass slides, flat pictures and posters, and I am told that these aids are used in most Canadian schools. There are more than one thousand schools in Ontario alone making use of them. Some idea of the extent of their work may be gathered from the fact that in ten years the film board has produced approximately 2,500 films, and has established a film library of more than 400 films in French and English. They have assisted in setting up 250 film councils and film libraries. There is a regular monthly showing of Canadian documentary films in some 500 theatres. The motion picture association of Canada estimates that in 1948 the national film board Canadian newsreel audience totalled 60 million people, and about 320 million in the United States.
I have not time to touch on the educational work that is being done by such organizations as the national museum where I understand about two-thirds of the exhibits have to be kept in the basement because of lack of space. Nor have I time to deal with
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy the national art gallery where again over half the pictures in their possession have to be stored in back rooms and basements because of lack of space to display them.
In the few minutes remaining at my disposal I want to turn to the broader issue of federal aid for education at every level. I submit there is now no question whatever about the feasibility of federal aid for education without interference with provincial rights. Two departments of the federal government have spent well over a quarter of a billion dollars in the past ten years on vocational education at the secondary school and university level. There has been no friction with the provincial governments on this score. The federal government has spent nearly $162 million in educating veterans. This work is now nearing completion, and the government will not be required any longer to spend these millions of dollars on their education. I submit that millions should now be available for aid to education within the provincially controlled schools of the nation.
For 1946 the total cost of provincially controlled schools in Canada was $186 million. An annual federal grant of $50 million to be allotted among the provinces would give education in Canada possibly the greatest fillip it has ever received with the exception of the educational work that was done in the forces during the war. That certainly would bring us closer to a realization of equal educational opportunity for all Canadian children; and that opportunity, I submit, should be limited only by the ability of the student to profit by it and the ability of the nation to provide it.
So I do urge the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to include on the agenda for the dominion-provincial conference to be held in January the question of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments in the matter of federal aid to education, thereby providing wider educational opportunities for more Canadian boys and girls. As I have said, no longer can there be any question of the willingness of provincial governments to accept federal aid for education, nor is there any question of their readiness to co-operate with the federal government in the administration and use of such aid for the benefit of those who are to be educated.
There can be no question as to the lack of equal educational opportunity in Canadian schools. Municipal and provincial governments, with the ever-increasing financial burdens which our constitution lays upon their doorstep, can no longer meet the educational requirements of our youth. Educational facilities vary as between province and province and even as between municipality and municipality within the same province. The

The Budget-Mr. Johnston educational opportunities available to a Canadian boy or girl today depend to a large extent upon the chance of being born and educated in one of our wealthier municipalities or provinces. That principle, I submit, is wrong, but it can be remedied only by aid for education given from the federal treasury to the provinces.
The inequalities of educational opportunity in Canada are ably set forth in a brief prepared by the Canadian teachers' federation, from which I should like to quote briefly in conclusion. In that brief, which was presented to the members of the cabinet last spring, they ask:
Is the government aware of the following facts?
(1)	That one out of every ten persons engaged In teaching Canadian children holds only a permit or temporary certificate, i.e. without the minimum professional qualifications normally demanded.
(2)	That the children of Canadians living in rural areas depend for their education upon the teachers whose services are purchased at an average salary of $1,207, whereas city children are taught by those with an average salary of $2,120. (Quebec not included in these averages because the figures are not available.)
(3)	That rural teachers are a transient group, the majority moving from one school to another (or out of teaching altogether) every two years or less, whereas the average tenure for teachers in urban schools is ten years.
(4)	That the latest available table (1947) showing median salaries reflects to a considerable degree the qualifications of teachers and gives some indication of the geographical differential in the matter of educational opportunity.
Median salaries-1947

Nova Scotia	 1,241

(5)	That despite the return of male teachers from the armed services, at the end of 1947 there were 1,700 fewer than in 1939.
(6)	That as of April, 1948, approximately 22,000 pupils in two provinces were receiving their education through correspondence courses because of the lack of teachers.
(7)	That 31 per cent of the teachers of one province and only 2 per cent of another are university graduates.
These statements are much more eloquent than I could possibly be with respect to the need for consideration at the next dominion-provincial conference of the question of federal aid to education.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I intend to deal with only one or two subjects, since it is not necessary for me to review at any length those important matters already dealt with by other members of the Social Credit party. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) dealt most effectively with the
[Mr. Noseworthy.)
agricultural problems of this country, and it is not necessary for me to repeat his arguments because he expressed the views of this party. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) ably dealt with the problems of foreign trade, pointing out the difficulties and suggesting remedies, and I need not discuss that matter.
I want to deal with a domestic matter which is becoming increasingly important. The hon. member for Acadia dealt with the condition of our trade relations with foreign countries, but that is not the only trade condition which is bad, or which is affecting this country. Some of our industrial concerns are facing trying times, entirely because of the policies of this government. Only the other day I saw a clipping from a United States publication, American Business, in which it was prophesied that by the end of 1951 over sixty per cent of the small businesses which had been started since the war, principally by returned men, would face failure. That is unfortunate because these men have invested their entire savings in these businesses, hoping to be able to make something of their lives after having fought in the war. It is interesting to note that I am not the only one concerned over the failure of businesses in this country. The other evening the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) described the situation which exists in his constituency and the adjoining riding. The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) also dealt with the situation in his constituency. Both hon. members referred to textile and woollen industries, which they said were laying off workers as a result of the devaluation policy of this government. But the matter of devaluation should be considered very carefully by the Conservative party, I think. Even before the Liberal party decided to devalue the dollar, the Conservative party had advocated the lowering of it. In the house tonight, the leader of the Progressive Conservative party reiterated his stand on that matter. I do not mention that in any spirit of criticism of the old line parties; I mention it to point out that this condition which exists in some of our industries and in the two constituencies to which I just referred is a condition which is brought about by the policies of this government as well as by the policies or suggestions of the Conservative party.
When the question of devaluation was brought up in the house, the Social Credit party opposed it. You will recall that back in 1945, when the Bretton Woods agreement was considered by this house, it was followed by the Geneva and Havana trade agreements. The results of these trade agreements are the

very conditions about which we are complaining today. The Conservative party, which is complaining about the deterioration in business and the closing up of factories, advocated those policies which have resulted in these conditions. The Conservatives supported the Liberal party on the Bretton Woods, Geneva and Havana trade agreements and those are the things that are causing the difficulties today. I think it would be well worth while if everyone in this house seriously considered the policies we are pursuing today, lest they have greater repercussions than those we have mentioned.
There is another industry, too, which needs a little attention. It is not only the industries in the constituencies to which reference has already been made that need attention, but in western Canada there is a business that is threatened with closing as a result of the policies of this government. It is the potteries at Medicine Hat in which two hundred and eighty people were employed, two hundred and thirty of whom have been laid off. I have just been handed the Medicine Hat News, which speaks about this very plant under the heading "Alberta Cabinet Hears Problem of Medalta Workers." This article is contained in the Medicine Hat News of Monday, October 31, 1949. It says:
The layoff developed a week ago as a result of devaluation of the pound sterling which resulted in eastern markets being offered British hotel and restaurant ware at twenty per cent under Canadian prices. Medalta is the largest Canadian manufacturer of this particular line, eighty per cent of its production being hotel ware.
It was forced to close production on all but a few special decorated lines. 230 of the total work force of 280 being laid off. On Friday some forty persons were called back to work with receipt of a large C.N.R. order. This staff is still on the job with no prospect of any greater increase in employment.
That is just another case in another part of Canada in which we find a failure in business due to the policies of this government.
Still further west, there is another industry which is facing grave difficulties. It was not more than two weeks ago, Mr. Speaker, that I had in my office a man engaged in the shipbuilding industry on the west coast. He pointed out some of the difficulties facing the shipbuilding industry in Canada. He said that this industry in Canada, so far as the west coast was concerned, was almost a thing of the past. His particular company was endeavouring to get into another line of production, so they would not be forced to close up entirely. Those are conditions that one views with alarm. They are conditions that have danger signs attached to them, and we should heed those signs.
I should like to read an extract concerning the shipbuilding industry which I believe
The Budget-Mr. Johnston was taken from the Ottawa Citizen. The heading is, "Government Studying Ways to Help Sagging Shipping Industry."
The government is considering ways of helping Canada's sagging shipping industry, but the policy is not expected to take shape for at least several months.
May I interject to say, Mr. Speaker, that almost anything can happen in those several months. Unless the government has a policy at hand, disaster may be the result. The articles continues:
Transport Minister Chevrier told the Commons last night that a number of plans are being considered on how to bolster the vital shipping industry.
"I wish I could say what those plans are, but I do not think it is in the public interest to do so," he said.
Farther down, the same article reads as follows:
Mr. Chevrier said he fully recognizes the seriousness of the shipping situation. But it was not a problem faced only by Canada. The same was true of every country in the world.
Increased cost of operation was one of the difficulties. Another was lack of freight and deterioration in freight rates. A third was devaluation.
Again we find in this shipbuilding industry the results of the policy pursued by this government. It seems to me that if this continues our country is in for a very bad time. For the ministers to say they are considering plans is not good enough. The government should have a definite plan to remedy this situation.
I should like to speak of another industry, one which is important not only to western Canada, but to Canada as a whole. It is facing grave difficulties and it is going to take more than just giving the matter consideration to remedy the problems facing the coal industry of western Canada. The member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) spoke about the condition in which that industry found itself in eastern Canada. I can assure him that the coal mining industry of western Canada is facing just as serious conditions as those faced by that industry in other parts of the country.
When we live in a country possessing about fourteen per cent of the world's known supply of coal, it seems to me we should be in a position to take advantage of that great industrial asset. No nation, at least up until today, has had great success industrially without using coal. There is talk about oil, but I believe the backbone of industrial power on the North American continent must be coal. We should, therefore, give every consideration to the maintenance and prosperity of that industry.
One of the conditions facing us in the west, and the same condition is facing the east, is that there is not the market locally for all the coal we can mine or all the coal we are mining. Even today, a great many

The Budget-Mr. Johnston coal miners are only working three or four days a week. In the interval, they have been living on their unemployment insurance. These benefits are nearly exhausted, so they will have to turn to relief. The prospects now are not very bright for anything else. The Canadian coal mining industry is in a deplorable state. It almost faces extinction unless something is done immediately to relieve that condition. There is a good market in Canada and why we do not take advantage of it is more than I can tell. In the central part of Canada, in the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec, we have an excellent market. Some hon. members may say to me, there may be some reason for your statement; they may say to me, the mines are so far off that it is not economically feasible to have the coal shipped down here and compete with coal coming from the United States. A condition has arisen in the United States through the coal strike which is being felt by all the industries in Canada. Should we allow our coal mines to be closed down and become dependent on a foreign nation for power to run our industries in central Canada? It seems to me to be the height of folly. Even though it might cost Canada a few million dollars to increase the subsidy on coal coming down here, I believe it would be a good investment in order to ensure the continuance of the production of the industries in central Canada. Even though a strike is on in the United States and even though devaluation of the dollar has taken place, yet it does not compensate the western coal dealers in sending coal down here to compete with United States coal. This is a time when we should be considering that problem seriously.
There is another important factor which should lead us to the preservation of our coal mining industry in Canada, namely, what would happen to us in time of war. We had an unfortunate experience of that during the last war when we were so short of coal because the United States refused to ship us any more inasmuch as they needed it themselves. If we allow our coal industry to close down, what will happen to us in a time of great national need? Just what happened during the last war. In this instance I do not think we should rely on a foreign nation for our coal supply.
There is another problem which will face us if we allow our coal industry to close down. Seven hundred thousand people are employed in the coal industry. If we allow the mines to close, even though oil production is increasing in the west, when we have a market here in eastern Canada, then we shall be faced with a tremendous unemployment problem, a problem that the federal govern-


ment will have to face sooner or later, because unemployment is becoming quite serious. It was estimated that there were over a hundred thousand employable unemployed on July 4. It is quite safe to say that there are at least 250,000 unemployed in Canada today. We cannot afford to have that number of unemployed climb much higher without serious repercussion in the country.
The cost of transportation is one of the difficult problems that we face in western Canada in order to obtain a market in central Canada. There are several factors which contribute to that high cost. The present freight rate alone on coal coming from the west is $8.33 a ton. On top of that we have the increased freight rates. The house will recall that the last increase the railways were asking for was 20 per cent. They received 8 per cent, but on coal they were allowed a straight 8 cents a ton flat increased rate. Just at a time when we really need a lower cost of transportation we have an increase in freight rates which could have been prevented by this government, making it still more difficult for us in western Canada to get our coal down to eastern Canada. It is true that the federal government pays a subsidy of $2.50 a ton on this coal; but even with that subsidy it is not possible to lay that coal down here and compete with Pennsylvania coal. If we allow that condition to prevail there is only one thing that is certain, namely, that our mines will close down.
It costs us between $16 and $18 a ton to lay down bituminous coal in Ontario. I should like to read a little clipping from the Financial Times of Friday, October 28, in regard to that question. It reads as follows:
Pressure Mounts for Coal Policy as Imports Stop Consumers Discover for Themselves High Transport Cost-Subvention Fails to Make Canadian Coal Fully Competitive
The article goes on to say:
Inquiries have therefore been made in Calgary and Edmonton, about the possibility of shipping coal from the foothills to Ontario. It was thought that increased costs of United States coal might finally have succeeded in making Alberta coal competitive in the east.
This does not seem to be the case, however. Although the would-be buyers of Alberta coal were favourably impressed with the prices that were quoted, and with the quality of the coal that was described to them both as to cleanliness and heating value, the cost of transportation threw all considerations out of gear. It costs $8.33 per ton, in carload lots, to get coal from Alberta to Ontario; and this after the subsidy paid by the government of $2.50 per ton.
Approximately one of every three tons of coal consumed in Canada is produced in this country. Particularly in the maritimes and, of course, throughout the western provinces, Canadian coal is burned to a very great extent in Quebec and to a greater extent in Ontario, the coal is almost exclusively

American. Most of the anthracite burned in Canada is American but, in the case of bituminous coal, the business is competitive, or would be competitive if the freight costs enabled Canadian mines to compete. At $8.33 per ton this is, of course, not likely, considering that United States coal comes to Canada largely in lake boats at much lower rates.
There are others who are concerned with the probable failure-I should not say "probable", I should say almost certain failure-of the coal mining industry, particularly in western Canada. It would not be an entire loss if the federal government were to raise the subvention on coal. They pay $2.50 a ton, but I am sure they could at least double that amount and still make it worth while from an all-Canadian standpoint. When you remember that we ship in $41 million worth of anthracite and $97 [DOT] 9 million worth of bituminous, making a total of $138-9 million from the United States each year, you can see that it would be a tremendous saving of United States dollars, and once again we would have the provinces both east and west coming to Canada's aid in the United States dollar shortage. I say even if we had to pay a much higher subsidy it would be to the federal government's financial advantage in the long run to increase the subsidy on western coal so that we would be able to put the coal down here in eastern markets and compete with the coal coming from the United States. The time has come, Mr. Speaker, for the federal government to consider a national coal policy, having in mind the things which I have suggested.
We are not overlooking the fact that oil is a keen competitor in the field of producing industrial power. We must recognize that probably oil development is going to be a very serious problem which must be dealt with in competition with coal. But from the standpoint of safety alone of the Dominion of Canada in time of war, and in other emergencies, it would be well worth our while to see that the coal mines of western Canada and Nova Scotia are kept in operation. In order to do that, it may be necessary to extend the research in the processing of coal, in an endeavour to extract oil or other by-products from it.
In a time of great emergency, in a time of war-particularly another war

it is very possible that this North American continent may become so isolated that it, including the United States, would not be able to get oil from any other outside source. It may stand us in good stead if we have developed the process in this country whereby we can get oil from coal, or use the coal in its natural form. In my opinion we dare not allow our coal mines to go.
I wish to read a brief article in connection with this subject entitled "Coal Industry
The Budget-Mr. Johnston Must Pay Attention to Oil". I read this to show that those who are interested in coalmining, including trade unions and others, are vitally concerned and recognize fully the competition that will come from oil. This dispatch from Sydney, Nova Scotia, states:
The coal industry must become a coal-into-oil industry or it is due for a serious and permanent decline, the United Mine Workers (C.C.L.) district 26 told the dominion coal board today.
In a brief, the union said the coal industry is headed for a decline because of the tremendous growth in the use of oil by industry, railways and residential consumers. The board is holding maritime sittings to hear various views on the industry.
It presented figures to show that in 1947 the mari-times consumed oil equivalent to 1,000,000 tons of coal, and that since 1943 oil consumption in the maritimes had increased by the equivalent of 350,000 tons of coal. During the same period coal consumptions declined by 600,000 tons.
The brief said the first step in development of an oil-from-coal industry in Cape Breton should be construction, at government cost, of a demonstration or pilot plant for experimentation. Fuel oil from coal now costs not more than three cents per gallon more than natural oil, the brief said. Operation of a commercial hydrogenation plant for experimentation would soon reduce this gap.
There is a good deal of truth in that. But whether the statement is based upon fact or not, surely our research branch in the dominion government could make very material progress in connection with the hydrogenation of coal in order to take the by-product of oil from it. This was done in Germany-in fact Germany almost conquered the world because of her highly mechanized armed forces which operated on oil produced from coal. So that what Germany could do, surely we could do, too.
There is one other subject with which I wish to deal briefly, namely that of old age pensions. I do not think I could go to sleep tonight and rest comfortably if I did not say a word for our senior citizens in Canada. I say this, not because I am partial to the subject at all-although I confess I am-but because it is within our physical potentialities to produce so much in this country that everyone should have the highest possible standard of living. That being so, I am not advocating anything the country cannot economically or financially do.
Our old age pensioners receive a maximum of $40. If every old age pensioner in Canada were to receive that maximum pension, they could not have anything but a very substandard living. When one considers the high cost of rent, coupled with the exceptionally high food costs-and they are still going higher and higher-there does not need to be any argument to convince every member in the house that it is an utter impossibility for human beings to exist decently on $40 a month.

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
But the old age pensioners of Canada do not all get that much. The Social Credit party- others too, but at least the Social Credit party-has advocated a minimum pension of at least $50 a month. We would be a sorry nation indeed if we could not produce enough in this country to give our old age pensioners at least that amount. These are the people who so faithfully worked all their years to build the Canada of which we are so proud; yet we turn them aside, with little thought, and with $40 a month, expecting them to exist on that pittance. It must indeed be an irritation and humiliation for these people to eke out their living on such a small amount.
We also advocate that the age for old age pensions should be lowered to 65 years for men and 60 years for women, and that when a husband qualifies for old age pension the wife too should automatically qualify. The reason is obvious. Usually the husband is the breadwinner, and when he has reached the age of three score and ten he is not capable of producing a living then for himself and his wife. As so often happens, however, the husband gets $40 a month-if he is lucky enough to get the maximum-and then the two of them must live on that $40. This makes it absurd.
Surely it should not require argument in the House of Commons to convince members that two people cannot live on $40. One could not have a decent living on it, so we should not expect two to do it. We say therefore that when the husband qualifies for the old age pension the wife should qualify automatically.
I believe old age pensions should be noncontributory. The only ones in Canada who are going to require assistance in their old age are going to be those who cannot possibly earn sufficient so that they may save enough to take care of themselves in their declining years. How in the world could we expect those people to contribute toward an old age pension?-and they are the only ones who will need it. It seems absurd to ask them to contribute out of their meagre savings so that they may obtain a pension upon reaching the age of seventy years.
Each one who at the present time is receiving an old age pension is contributing every day of his life very materially, because each time he buys an article from his old age pension allotment he is making a substantial contribution to the income of Canada, and to the consolidated revenue fund. Therefore let it not be said that the old age pensioners, or those who will come under pension provisions in years to come, are not making their contributions, even at this time. We say therefore that the old age pension should be
[Mr. Johnston.l
non-contributory. I do not want to keep the house any longer, but I did want to say those few words.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING RENT CONTROL

speechtext:
Hon. Douglas Abbot! (Minister of Finance):
Mr. Speaker, if I could have the unanimous consent of the house to revert to motions, I should like to make a statement respecting rent control.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING RENT CONTROL
speechtext: Has the minister the unanimous consent of the house?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING RENT CONTROL
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE RESPECTING RENT CONTROL
speechtext:
For some time now the government has been considering what action should be taken with respect to rent control when the present legislation expires. As hon. members are aware, the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, will expire on March 31, 1950, or sixty days after parliament first meets during the year 1950, whichever date be the earlier.
Just about a year ago-to be exact, on October 23, 1948-I wrote to the premiers of each of the provincial governments, advising them that the federal government was prepared to vacate the field to any province which might decide to undertake rent control. I offered, on behalf of the government, to make available to any province the records, information, experience and staff of the rentals administration and also, subject to parliament's approval, to pay the cost of any provincial rental administration for one year. At the same time I reminded the provincial premiers that the constitutionality
Rent Control
of federal rent control had been questioned and was before the courts, and referred to the situation that would arise should federal rent control be held to be invalid.
None of the then existing provinces was prepared to undertake rent control. On the other hand, when Newfoundland joined Canada it retained its own system of rent control.
In offering to vacate the field to the provinces a year ago the federal government was not seeking to relieve itself of responsibility for rent control. It was motivated solely by concern for the situation that would arise should rent control be held to be beyond the constitutional powers of the federal authorities. It believed at that time that the sudden end of rent control would result in unnecessary disruption and hardship, and it offered to put the matter beyond doubt by giving the provinces an opportunity to introduce legislation that could not be successfully challenged in the courts.
May I say at this point that the advice which the government receives from its law officers is that the existing federal regulations with respect to rent control are valid. But in a matter which concerns the welfare of so many Canadians the government would not be discharging its responsibilities to the people of Canada as it should if it did not take every precaution. It is possible that the courts would decide that our regulations are unconstitutional. We cannot disregard that possibility.
If there was uncertainty about the position a year ago, there is at least the same degree of uncertainty today. The government has therefore decided to refer the question of the validity of the rental regulations to the supreme court, in the hope and expectation that a decision will be given before the present legislation expires. As I have said, the law officers of the crown are of opinion that the rentals regulations are valid. They are also of opinion that both the law and the facts support the view that it lies within the authority of parliament to extend these regulations for a further period. Counsel will be instructed by the Attorney General of Canada to press this view before the court. The order in council making the reference is being prepared and when approved will be tabled in this house.
If no unfavourable decision is given, the government at the next session will ask parliament to grant a further extension of the rentals regulations. The government intends to continue with its program of orderly decontrol as rapidly as conditions warrant but we do not believe that this program can be completed before March 31, 1950. Let me make it quite clear that the purpose of clarifying the

Rent Control
legal position is not to perpetuate federal rent control. On the contrary, the purpose is to confirm our authority to proceed in an orderly way towards the eventual withdrawal of all controls. This has been our firm policy towards wartime controls in general and rent control is no exception.
Should the supreme court find that the rentals regulations are now beyond the powers of parliament, then of course a different situation arises. I am accordingly writing at once to the premiers of the provinces acquainting them with our intention and offering to assist in the preparation of what might be termed "stand-by" legislation if they wish to present such legislation to their respective legislatures.
After the most careful consideration of all the alternatives, the government believes that this course of action is the best. We believe that gradual and orderly decontrol is the right policy. At any time, however, that policy could be frustrated by an adverse decision of the courts. Such a decision might come at a most inconvenient time when the provinces might not be in a position to act as they see fit in the interests of their residents. By referring the question to the supreme court before the present legislation expires and by giving ample notice of our intention to do so, such a situation can, we hope, be avoided.
I should add that the federal government, of course, continues to stand ready at any time to vacate the field of rent control to any province which makes a formal request to that effect. We do not wish to stand in the way of any province which desires to operate in the field of rent control.
I also wish to take this opportunity of announcing some further measures of decontrol.
We have made some progress in the direction of decontrol since the end of the war, but a very high proportion of tenanted dwellings is still subject to the rentals regulations and maximum rentals are undoubtedly still well below the levels that would be established in a free market. Before the rentals regulations are completely withdrawn I hope that there will be some further improvement in the housing situation, and I think it fair to say that no other country is overcoming its housing shortage more quickly. Nevertheless, it seems probable that rentals might well settle eventually at a level substantially above the present maximum levels provided in our regulations. Sooner or later the adjustment must be made, and, as I have said, it is our policy to permit this adjustment to be made gradually rather than abruptly.

The rentals regulations are accordingly being amended as follows:
(1)	Rentals for rooms, parts of houses and the like, in which a tenant is required to share toilet facilities or some other similar equipment, may be increased by not more than 20 per cent. I should point out that there have been no previous general increases in maximum rentals for this kind of accommodation since the introduction of rent control. Landlords of such accommodation are also being given the right to terminate any lease on six months' notice. These changes do not apply to per person rates, that is, to rates which include services such as the provision of furniture, linen and so forth. There is already a sufficient degree of flexibility in the present regulations applying to per person rates.
(2)	Landlords will be permitted to offer a term certain lease for not less than one year in consideration of a rental increase of not more than 20 per cent in the case of unheated self-contained dwellings and of not more than 25 per cent in the case of heated self-contained dwellings. This lease must contain a clause permitting the tenant to terminate it at one month's notice. If the tenant refuses the offer the landlord may require him to vacate under the laws of the province and the accommodation then becomes free of federal rent control.
(3)	Landlords and tenants may enter into term certain leases of not less than two years' duration at any rental upon which they may agree. The rentals administrator has already given approval to about 2,500 joint applications by landlord and tenant to enter into such two-year leases. Hereafter these two-year leases will not require the specific approval of the administrator.
(4)	Landlords who owned accommodation prior to November 1, 1949, will be enabled to gain possession for their own use as a residence on giving six months' notice declaring their need. Until now landlords have had this right only in respect of accommodation which they owned prior to November 1, 1947. The rule that such notices may not expire during the winter months is also being withdrawn. It is not retroactive, of course, so that none of the notices already given will expire during the coming six months' period.
These are the major changes being made at the present time. They will become effective by orders of the wartime prices and trade board, as from December 15, 1949. A number of other sundry changes are also being made and they will be announced in the usual way when the orders themselves are completed and published.

May I add one final word to which I hope the press will give some prominence. In order to carry out the changes which have been announced it will be necessary to print and distribute many thousands of forms. They will be made available as quickly as possible. Even under the most favourable circumstances, however, some time will elapse before every rentals office in the country has an adequate supply on hand. This necessary delay will not in any way affect the rights of landlords or tenants because, as I have said, the orders do not become effective until the middle of next month. My advice to the general public therefore is to wait for a further announcement by the rentals administration before applying to local offices for the forms and other details.
